title: Tales, Stories and Daydreams of Mama Martina and Antonito
author: Freddy Córdova Ossio
translation_note: Translated from the original Spanish. Song lyrics are kept in Spanish.

blocks.text: This book is not a linear story. It is a weaving of memories, voices and dreams, like the threads on a loom that cross one another to form a single cloak.

In these pages the stories of Mama Martina, a midwife and wise curandera (healer) from the valleys of the Imperial Town (Villa Imperial) of Potosí, live side by side with the dreams of Antonito, who converses with masters of art and of the spirit. They are tales that seem to be fragments of different times, yet they share a single heartbeat: respect and affection for our ancestors.
Each tale is a moment held still: a setting, a walk, a workshop. They are scenes that do not seek to be fully explained, but to be felt, because in them lies hidden the root of who we are.
And so memory and dream intertwine to remind us that the past does not die, but goes on teaching in the voices of our grandparents and in the dreams of children.
The Inheritance of Love

My name is Antonito. I am the great-grandson of Mama Martina and Abrahán Ossio, a respected healer and midwife and a cabinetmaker of the Valley of Potosí, where I was born. Both were known for a great deal of work, recognized and vouched for by its results and its creativity, and also for being humble and honest people with the folk of the town and with the families of the Spanish miners.

I have always considered myself the luckiest and most beloved great-grandson of all, for being with them and keeping them company in their daily tasks. At six years old I helped in the carpentry shop, and I helped Mama Martina prepare her medicines from herbs and earths. Today we are walking along rocky paths, searching for herbs and earths and learning about them, and talking about her past life: the events, histories, tales and legends from the historical past of our colonial land. These stories, told by her and by my sister, have in some way strengthened my spirit of struggle and perseverance. Without them I believe I would have failed in all my purposes and in my wish to better myself. Above all, they have made me proud of my family as the bearers of that spirit of struggle and sacrifice. My honor and eternal gratitude to them.

I remember that my parents worked gathering ore in Atocha and Tasna and sold it to the ore buyers, and my mama Martina sometimes sold vegetables she got in Cotagaita and delivered the babies of many of her comadres. We were very happy; I never lacked for anything. Then one day we got up very early, and they told me to bring my dog Tobías. In a loud voice my tata said: we are going to travel very far, we need our Tobías to protect us, we will go to a quieter place to work, we can't stay here any longer. They charged me with a whole list of things… to look after myself, to protect myself from other people, always to be polite, willing, attentive and respectful with my elders, not to lie, and not to pick up anything that wasn't mine, even if it had been thrown away. I don't know why they told me this over and over again.

We set out in the small hours of the morning with bags on our backs, carrying our provisions for many days, water, coca tea, and a metal grinder for the ore, which we loaded onto the llama. Our Tobías walked ahead. It seemed like a fiesta, the way he barked and jumped, as if he could sense freedom. We marched for days; my feet were sore. We went on along narrow, stony paths, the trail of the miners and their llama trains, resting now and then, until we reached the foot of the river, and across from it stood the town of Atocha, where gold and silver were mined. We went on about two leagues farther and stayed in the ravine, a place where we could pick ore (apallar) and search freely and find what we were looking for… This rocky ravine was surrounded by paja brava, yareta and churqui grown very tall. We sat down to rest and then walked the rest of the way. I set about clearing the ground to spend the night, and gave the llamas food, after tying them up and securing them so they wouldn't bolt. We ate our provisions and drank a little coca tea; Tobías shared our food with us. The weather was sunny and a little cloudy, with an icy wind blowing, but it was bearable. After chewing coca, my parents went off to find a place to settle and grind or sift the ore, silver and gold. Whenever they sat down, it was a sign that they had found the right place, the one they were looking for. When I saw this, I had to set about finding food. In the time we stayed there I saw many wild guinea pigs (cuis), and turtledoves that came to drink water at the stream that ran close by… Tobías, Tobías, come on, let's go, I want you to help me hunt. As if he understood, he nodded his head; he was like a person. He jumped and barked and barked, as if to say, what joy!… Don't bark, don't bark, I kept telling him, to make him hush. We kept walking, until suddenly we heard the flutter of a dove flying off a short distance. We followed it: it will tire, it will tire. Tobías, follow it, I signal to him, and you can catch it. He runs like a gazelle, silently, and I wait a little while, and then I hear him barking, and soon he appears with the dove in his mouth. I stroke him and run my hand over his head: very good, Tobías, now we have something to eat today. We kept looking, and after a while we saw a cuis running. Run, run, Tobías, don't lose it, careful it doesn't get into its burrow! It was amazing. Tobías was so agile, a true hunter; he caught it and brought it to me and laid it in my lap. Bravo, Tobías! I gave him a kiss and he began to bark and jump. You have your food too. Then I cut the little necks of both, and a lot of bright red blood came out, which I drank from both of them. We shared with Tobías; I told him, open your mouth, and you should have seen how he enjoyed it, licking himself right up to his nose. Next I had to look for firewood or yareta. A few steps away I found some; it was quite dry. I tied it up and carried it on my back to our resting place. I took some evenly shaped stones, made my kjoncha and laid the yareta and the firewood in it. Striking some stones that we had gotten from the miners, which make sparks and fire, I managed it. I ran to the river with my clay pot, fetched water and brought it to a boil for the dove and the rabbit, so as to skin them and pluck the feathers right away, because if you don't do it at that moment it's hard; they turn stiff. I took out the insides of both and gave them to Tobías with all the giblets. I told him: eat, eat as if it were the last time. I ran a stick through the dove and the cuis and then cooked them over a slow fire, turning them every so often. Soon you could smell the roasting meat. I also put the little potatoes and chuños in another pot to boil, and a while later everything was ready to eat. When the sun was going down, that was when my tatas, which in Quechua means my parents, were due back. Martinita, we're home! What joy to hear them. Tobías announced their safe arrival with his barking… Mamitay, papituy, how happy I am to see you… Martinita, what have you done? We smell meat, where did you get it… Martinita tells them the whole story. Help yourselves, it's nice and hot, eat this little dove and the rabbit… How delicious, dear daughter, we are so pleased. Give me a little coca tea and we'll rest. We'll tell you that we've found a good little vein, so we have to work hard, and for that we'll get our kokawi (provisions for the road) ready so we can leave very early. I want you to take care of yourself; don't let Tobías wander too far, so that he can look after you. And so a few days went by. They always came back happy, and they said again that in two days we would go to the town.

The next day she wakes to the barking. Her parents had already left. She went on with the routine of finding food and preparing it, but she felt a weight on her chest, as if something were happening to her. She also heard Tobías howling. What's wrong with you, what have you seen, what are you sensing? She heard the little birds, the Parachí Dios, singing on and on, which they usually do when a very heavy rain is coming; I had learned that from my mother. Some time passed and it began to cloud over. The weather turned ugly and cold, with a lot of wind and black clouds; it looks like a real storm is coming. Time went by, and every so often a sadness, a despair, came over me. In my little head I say: let them come, they must be cold and hungry by now. Please, Lord, take care of them, I beg you… In the dark sky there are flashes of lightning with a deafening noise, and a few drops of rain. Please let them come, let them come soon. A while later I hear barking, which is a sign they are near. They appear and I run to meet them, a little wet. How good that you've come, papitos! I made you a very hot lawita and your little cup of tea, so you can rest afterwards. The thunder and lightning grow stronger and stronger. After we finish eating, a very heavy rain comes down. We cover ourselves with hides, I lie close to my Tobías, and we fall asleep….

I don't know how much time passed…. I wake up with my head very heavy. I heard desperate shouting and weeping, people crying out: look, look at the state they're in, they're all dead, dead… I didn't know if I was dreaming. I couldn't move, neither my arms nor my feet; they seemed paralyzed. I heard what they were shouting, but I couldn't open my eyelids. I heard them saying: don't go near, don't go near, they're charged, the grown-ups are badly burned, and the little girl and the dog have no burns, but they may be marked by the lightning's charge. With great difficulty I manage to move my arms and feet. She's moving, she's moving! the people shout. Don't go near, it's very dangerous, it could kill us!... Sleep comes over me again. I don't know how long I stayed in that state. I wake up to the barking of my Tobías, who was licking my face and whimpering…. I ask myself: what has happened to me? I don't feel well, my head seems hollow. It seemed I was still dreaming. I came to my senses because Tobías was tugging at my clothes. Only then do I think: this is not a dream. What has happened to me? Where are my parents? Have they already gone to work? I don't see them. Just then a palliri appears (one of the women who pick ore by hand): Daughter, we thought you were dead and we were very afraid to touch you, because of the danger of the lightning that left a charge in you. You've been lying here for about three days beside your little dog. We have to tell you… those people… were your parents. Yes, yes, where are they? They've died, the lightning killed them. No, no! I screamed and screamed. Calm down, daughter, we buried them over there, we couldn't leave them like that. I didn't know what to answer; I could only weep and weep. It seemed like a lie. All I could do was scream and scream, and hear my Tobías howling. Only then did I kneel down, hugging my dog, and scream and scream: Lord, why have you done this to me? You leave me alone, alone. What am I going to do now? Where am I going to go? You told me you would always be with me, and now who am I going to cook for, dance for and make laugh? Lord, give me strength to bear this punishment… Don't cry, daughter, it is a sorrow for us too….. We found this bag beside them and we want to give it to you. It's very heavy; surely it has their ore and other things for grinding. We'll leave it with you. Look for us whenever you need us. We're also leaving you this bit of food and tea so you can have something. And they walked away, disappearing into the horizon.

In the morning I go to the place where my parents' remains lay, as if someone were guiding me…. I get there, and on my knees with my hands on the earth, I asked them, weeping: why have you abandoned me? But I am sure you will always be at my side, protecting me. I am leaving this place; I will follow the path you guide me on. I take with me the charge you gave me and the bag, to face my days… As she leaves, she asks herself what has become of our llama. Tobías, let's go look for it. They spend some time walking among the stones and the paja brava, and there ahead we find the llama on its knees, eating shrubs. Come on, come on. They load it with all its things and her parents' bag. They walk and walk through different places, heedless of time, until they reach a mild town full of greenery called Cotagaita… to face another reality, alone with her Tobías….

Martina was barely eight years old when destiny tested her with its hardest lesson: to face the road of life with nothing but her own strength. She learned early that from loss, too, springs the root of love and strength.

Hunger and fear were her only companions, but so were hope and the strength to work. From then on I learned to sell my vegetables, toasted broad beans, kispiña and medicinal plants, and many people came up to me and bought what I had, and so I was able to feel a little calmer. My Tobías kept me company in all this; he never left my side for a moment... A long time passed in this routine, days of great sadness, but always with the strength to fight and keep going, with the strength and hope her parents had instilled in her…

One very sunny morning, under a clear sky, with the song of the little birds flying from tree to tree as if to show me their joy, an old woman with silver hair suddenly came up to me. Her voice made me tremble, and I had the feeling that I had always seen her or known her. She said to me: Child, I am interested in everything you have; how much is it? I'll buy it all… But, señora… She would not let me answer. Tell me how much it is and I'll pay you, don't worry, don't be surprised at what I'm telling you, don't hesitate… I did not know what to say, and she handed me the money I named; it was the whole week's sales. Shall I carry it to your house... would you like me to? Very well, child, let's go... Tell me, what is your name? She repeated, what is your name? And I answered without fear: Martina. Martina, señora, and you? Aurora de la Cruz. My parents brought me from Toledo, which is in the Old World, and I stayed. I live alone and devote myself to healing and to attending births. And where do you live?… In the countryside, and I sell food and these plants and earths that my mama used very often. And so they walked a good stretch. My heart was pounding at all this and I could not explain it; I walked as if I were outside myself. Suddenly we stopped, and the señora, with great delicacy and a very slow step, showed me that from this street the next one was close by. This is my house, she said: it had an immense gate and a white-painted front. If you like, you can come another day. Come, keep me company, you could be my companion…. Her voice was so refined and respectful. It was a very large and luxurious house. If you wish, and if you trust me, go and bring your little things, whatever you have… I was left very surprised and thoughtful… something drew me to her, as if it were the spirit of my parents. Suddenly a certain affection and attraction was born in me, as if she were of my own blood. I told her: I'll go to the countryside and come back…. And on the way it was as if a light shone on me; something gave me such confidence. I had nothing more to think over twice, and I came back the next day with the little I had. She welcomed me with joy and open arms, kissing me on the forehead: You will be my daughter, which is what I have always wanted. You are very beautiful, with mischievous blue eyes. This is your home, and I offer you this room so you can settle in. You will not leave; you are part of me… I did not know what to say or how to answer…. It was as if I were dreaming, and finding the peace and calm of being beside my beloved parents… As the shadows of night came on, I remembered, and grieved over, the loss of my faithful friend, my dog Tobías, who had kept me company for years of my life, ever since I lost my parents... Later that night I heard Doña Aurora's voice. She asked me: Do you know how to say the prayer…. the one we say when it is time to rest, so as to wake up with great strength, hope and faith in the Lord for the day, so that things go well for us… I answered no… That's how it is... listen, and when I am away you must always say it… I listened closely to how she prayed, with such faith that tears even came to her eyes, and she asked that I never be separated from her and that my health be kept safe. From that declaration I truly knew that she loved me, that she did so from the depths of her being… She told me: Tomorrow I'll leave very early and I may be gone two days; you make your own meals, and don't worry about me…. But señora, let me go with you. No, no. Later on you'll tire of our work…. Some days after she returned she asked me: How do you know about medicinal plants… My mama taught me to use them for some illnesses and pains. Very good, we share the same calling, so it won't be hard for you to come out with me and see a lot of people. First of all, I want you to put on these clothes that I bought some days ago; that way I will feel very proud to introduce my dear daughter to the people I know, and they will recognize you and respect you as such. What she declared surprised me, and I felt much more affection for her. From that moment on she taught me how to recognize and cure the ailments of each one of her patients; some of them I already knew from my mama's guidance. In this endeavor I was with her day and night, going with her to the countryside and on her rounds. She was very responsible and punctual, no matter whether her patients were country people or townsfolk.

One day she took me to see a boy, perhaps about 12 years old, lying on some sheepskins, his gaze lowered, his eyes without shine, his little face sad, pale and utterly wasted, his little hands bony, his eyes sunken, as if he had never eaten or been given any food. This boy is a treasure…. she repeated it with such tenderness… The woman in charge said he had been like this ever since his papa died in the mine, and his mama was sick in the lungs. The doctors from the mining camp had seen him; he responded to nothing. Doña Aurora said again, almost sobbing: It is as if I were standing before my own son…. I feel his suffering deeply. She asked the woman in charge to prepare food: Right now I want you to bring me a jug of goat's milk, and give it to him every day. Son, she said to him in a soft, sure voice, offering him her trust and affection, I'll take you home, I'll care for you as if you were my beloved son. She kissed him on the forehead and on his little hand, and, closing her eyes, she repeated three times: Lord, Lord, Lord, give health and strength to my child. As if it were an awakening, a soft voice was heard saying: Thank you, my señora, thank you. And, trembling, he tried to get up, and with a smile he hugged and kissed her, and tears could be seen on his cheeks. That instant made my whole body shudder, and I saw her weeping with the boy; my heart broke and I could not hold back my tears. This showed me that she was a very sincere, honest and humble woman, who offered inner peace to everyone who came near her. From that moment the boy began to receive his milk and his care. As time and care went on, he could be seen to be happier and to have hope of living; the moment the boy saw Dña. Aurora, a shine came into his eyes and a smile expressing his gratitude. We came back many weeks later and saw him walking; with firmer little steps and open arms he went to the señora, kissed her on the forehead and said thank you, and may the Lord repay you... What an improvement, simply from offering him spiritual strength and trust; that was the medicine that set him on the road to his cure… At that instant, without thinking, it came from the depths of my being, and I said to her: Mamita Aurora, what have you done for the boy… She answered me slowly... and I saw the tears welling from her leaden-gray eyes: Thank you, child, how long I have waited for that to come from your mouth and your heart, for you to call me mamita.. for me it is a joy and a blessing... Child, I want you to know that the soul is like the plants… the first needs trust, love and hope, and the plants need water and sun; without these they wither and die…… You are the breath of my life... and the light of my hope…

Many weeks went by. I had grown used to her manners, her ways; it seemed I had always known her. We ate together and laughed over some mischief or other, above all about her patients. One quiet night, as we sat drinking cedrón tea: Child, child Martina… I felt a kind of shiver run through my body, and at the same time peace and security. What could she want to tell me? Has she grown tired of me, or what can it be? She spoke in a calm but sure voice: You have never told me about your parents or where you come from. Tell me, and if you'd rather not, I leave it up to you… I never told anyone, and no one ever asked me, what happened to me. I remember that my papas worked picking ore at my Atocha-Tasna and sold it to the ore buyers, and my mama sometimes sold vegetables she got in Cotagaita and delivered babies for some of the comadres. We were very happy; I never lacked anything. And one day we got up very early, and they told me to bring along my dog Tobías. In a loud voice my tata says: We are going to travel very far, we need our Tobías to protect us, we'll go somewhere else to work, we can't stay here any longer. They charged me with a whole list of things: to look after myself, to protect myself from other people, always to be willing, attentive and respectful toward older people, not to lie, and never to pick up anything that isn't yours, even if it has been thrown away. I don't know why they told me these things over and over again./1/

We set off before dawn, with bags on our backs, carrying food for many days, water, coca tea, a metal grinder for the ore, which we loaded onto the llama, and in front went Tobías, our dog. It seemed like a fiesta, the way he barked and leaped, as if foretelling freedom. So she told, with great sadness and weeping, what had happened in her childhood…. We marched for days on aching feet, along narrow, stony trails traveled by the miners and their llamas, resting now and then, until we reached the banks of the river, and across from it stood the town of Atocha, where gold and silver were mined. We went on some two leagues further and stayed in the ravine, a place where we could glean ore (apallar) or search freely and find what we were looking for. And so she went on with her story and the sad end of her parents… weeping and repeating: Why did this happen to me? I dreamed of them, and of growing up, of having a future without sadness, tears and hardship. The only one I shared this suffering with was my dog Tobías, who later left me as well, and that was another time of suffering, and I had little hope of going on
living…

Doña Aurora, full of admiration…. Child, you are a heroine, brave, with a star that guides you. For that reason I choose you, and you have appeared on my path. I do not regret it, and I say it again: I call you my daughter. You are the owner of, and the one responsible for, everything we have. We will always be together until the end. For me it is a joy and a source of pride to have you at my side; it is what was missing in my lonely life… The days went by, and time, and between the two of them grew such closeness and respect that no one could doubt they were a happy family.…

From the meeting of those two souls was born the strength of a tradition that can still be breathed in the memory of the valleys... Doña Aurora, in their moments of rest and with peace in her heart, would tell her all the stories of her grandparents and parents, so that she would keep them in mind and they would serve her as experience over the course of her life… …….
The Slave Trade and Slavery in the Americas

The transatlantic slave trade in colonial times was one of the most lucrative businesses, making fortunes at the cost of the misery of Black people. That is why the trade in Africans is described as a true industry. It is estimated that from 1481 to 1517 thousands of slaves were sent to the New World by order of the Spanish hierarchy, and that its ships carried approximately three million to South America. They arrived in Cuba, Brazil and the Río de la Plata, where they were offered to buyers who put them to domestic work, hauling loads and mining. Before reaching their destination they walked like pack trains, tied together or in wooden collars so they could not escape.

The slaves were indispensable to the overall progress of these countries. Coming from the west coast of Africa, from the Congo, Nigeria and New Guinea, they were carried in special ships [slave ships], also called Coffins or Tumbeiros. These names expressed the character of all those mercantile expeditions, because only half of the Africans who had left Africa arrived alive in America. They traveled tied up and crammed into the ships' holds, without the most basic hygiene, since they had to relieve themselves in the same place, and without proper food. In these conditions, out on the high seas, those Africans fell prey to starvation, dehydration, gastrointestinal infections and hunger; packed together and exhausted, they died in the midst of their companions. Some, to escape their mistreatment, threw themselves into the sea and drowned or were devoured by sharks.

In the trade in Africans the price or cost varied a great deal. For example, in the Río de la Plata a Black slave was sold for 80 pesos fuertes, while in Potosí, a true devourer of human beings in its mines, he was resold at a price of 300 to 400 pesos; this high price benefited the Basques, the only ones wealthy enough.

At first the few, costly African slaves were put to work on haciendas, in the silver mills (ingenios) and in artisans' workshops, and some served as overseers or foremen; if they had certain qualities that interested their masters, they held a favored position compared with the Indigenous workers.

The true and principal pioneer owners of slaves were the religious orders. The living conditions of enslaved men and women were harsh. On religious properties the Africans were kept under constant control so that they would not form families or become pregnant; their condition determined that of their descendants, and the child of a slave woman was born a slave. The slaves were subjected to every kind of labor; young women were treated entirely as sexual objects. Women and men over 45 were given their freedom, by then sick and without strength and often without family, and they joined the mass of the unemployed and the street. Many of them were taken in by relatives or sheltered by acquaintances until their old age, and others died on the outskirts of the town.

Over time they organized themselves in order to stay closer together and so preserve their customs, beliefs, language and so on. From this arose the famous Cofradías, or brotherhoods; among these the first were those devoted to a saint, such as San Benito, and they were watched over by the Church.

Black people served according to the labor needs of the European colonists, on agricultural plantations and in mining; they formed the base of the Ibero-American economy and, through it, the support of the Spanish and Portuguese crowns. For every African who reached these shores alive, mortality was so great that five perished, as we have already mentioned, from starvation, diarrhea, dehydration, suicide or various punishments.
On the Life of Black People in Colonial Potosí

My grandfather used to tell me that many of the Black people brought from Africa were made to work in the mines, and they could not bear the cold and died. In those years, as a result of a snowfall that lasted 8 days and a very piercing icy wind, and because the houses gave so little protection, 14 Spaniards and 18 Black slaves died.

Years later, the Black slaves who worked at the furnaces of the Royal Mint (Casa de la Moneda), as silver smelters and coin minters, were kept under a system of strict confinement, above all to prevent the theft of silver and the street fights between groups of Africans and Indians. In 1645 it was discovered that the enslaved Black women of the town came into the Mint to fetch water from the fountain, and that it was they who carried out the silver the slaves handed them. When discovered, they were subjected to harsh punishments such as 100 lashes. Many often escaped because of the mistreatment, the hunger or the pains they felt in their legs, which they found very severe; many of them became paralyzed, and this was grounds for dismissal. Even so, they often went to the Mint on various pretexts to get close to the overseers and overpower them, and many times they caused their deaths, which they considered the only way to seek their freedom. Otherwise, from the complications of their ailments, they died in the gloomy, dark and cold dungeons of the Mint, which had windows barred with steel.

The Black slaves had a wealth of energy and daring. They carried out their masters' wishes, playing many roles, as hired killers, torturers, executioners or poisoners, and many, men and women alike, were used as sexual objects. From this arose the tantanacus, the forming of couples accepted or not by the family or the group, as in the case of the Basques.

Many of the Africans who worked in the mines or in the Mint complained of intense pains in their limbs, their head or their abdomen; blows they received accidentally at their work caused these ailments. Some died suddenly and others were left permanently disabled, while others endured the pain to keep on with their tasks and so avoid the overseers' lashes.

Over time, and in different periods, mixtures arose between whites, Blacks and Indians, and the CASTAS were formed: social systems in which a person's status is assigned for life. Therefore, in societies organized by castas the different strata are closed, and the individual must remain in the social stratum into which he was born. The following castas are identified:
A white and an Indian produce a Mestizo
A white and a Mestizo produce a Criollo
A white and a Black produce a Mulato
A white and a Mulato produce a Cuarterón
An Indigenous person and a Black produce a Zambo
A Mulato and a Spaniard produce a Marisco
A Castizo and a Spanish woman produce a Español
A Chino and an Indian woman produce a Salta Atrás
A Salta Atrás with a Mulata produces a Loba
A Marisco with a Spanish woman produces a Chino
A Lobo with a China produces a Jíbaro
A Jíbaro with a Mulata produces an Albarazado
An Albarazado with a Negra produces a Carbajo
A Calpamulato with a Carbura produces a Tente en el Aire
A Tente en el Aire with a Mulata produces a No te Entiendo, etc...

A very interesting example is the parentage of Marshal Andrés de Santa Cruz: his parents were the criollo Santa Cruz Villavicencio and his wife, a slave named Juana Basilia Calahumana, daughter of the Cacique of Huarina, 52 years of age, whom he bought for a price of 150 pesos [Ref. Crónicas potosinas].
Of their customs there remain, among their dances, the candombe, and among their dishes, mondongo, achuras, locro and mazamorras.

These stories show us that the pursuit of wealth has no borders and no scruples whatsoever. Every right of a family or community is ignored; people are kidnapped without regard for any feeling, for love, or for their responsibilities as members of a family. There was utter abuse and, above all, arrogance toward those peoples whose traditions and customs were disregarded. They were treated as true animals; under the influence of religion it was said they had no SOUL, and therefore they should be treated as beasts. Neither age nor sex was taken into account for the work they had to do. They contracted many illnesses, from infections to deficiency diseases, and even more because of the altitude: circulatory problems, gangrene, sexual abuse, and they were abandoned when they no longer met their masters' demands or economic interests. This is a true lesson from our forebears, and one that in the future will be regarded as an element of struggle and liberation……
The War of the Vicuñas and the Basques

The thriving economy of the Villa Imperial, built above all on mining, drew the interests of the viceroyalty and the hopes of many groups, families as well as mining enterprises. It also drew the ships that carried Black people, Arabs and even former convicts, for this was a way of getting rid of murderers and of prisoners jailed for all sorts of offenses who would otherwise have had to spend years behind bars; and since it also brought in a great deal of money, the authorities decided to grant concessions to the navigators and to some of the pirates who came to the Indies and to the Villa Imperial in search of treasure. Above all it was the Biscayans who were the most eager and the most favored in the concessions, and who cornered the silver mills, the mines and trade in general.

These facts were the cause of the dispute and the clashes known as the War of the Basques (Vascongados) and the Vicuñas, the latter represented by the Indians, criollos, mestizos, mulatos and others under the leadership of Alonzo de Ibáñez. The fighting took place in the Pampa de San Clemente and broke out every day, in brawls, sword thrusts and assaults, and it would last three years. There was no end to the hatred and the feuding between the Basque settlers and the so-called peninsulares, Arabs, Italians and Dutch, and the criollos descended from Spaniards, who were called Vicuñas. The economic and social situation grew tenser and tenser. The natural deposits of silver and tin brought a flood of people who wanted to work and make their fortune, but the economic, social and political dominance of the Basques, who formed a powerful group that acted as it pleased and on a whim, and who carried themselves with great pride and arrogance, bred hatred among the population, including the mitayos, the enslaved Black people, and even people of their own Iberian stock, and this led to quarrels and feuds.

These events, which also came together with a decline in silver production, caught the attention of Don Francisco Toledo in a surprising way: the murder of Don Juan de Urbieta by the Vicuñas on June 8, 1622. The following night the Basques patrolled the Villa, saying in their own tongue: “Whoever does not answer in Basque must die.” There were skirmishes on both sides, and even an attempt at peace on June 22. After that the war went on with its ups and downs, favorable at first to the Vicuñas, warriors and soldiers of fortune more used to handling weapons. The Basque leaders found themselves forced to leave Potosí and settle in La Plata, where they were close to the authorities and where they had strong ties through the silver trade. Upon the arrival of the Viceroy of Peru, Philip IV, the Spanish monarch, ordered Diego Fernández de Córdoba to put to death some forty Vicuña leaders between 1624 and 1625. Later an attempt was made to bring peace through the marriage of the daughter of Don Alláname to the son of Castillo, one of the captains of a band of Vicuñas.
In spite of this, the feuding went on, and above all the Basques persisted in their great ambition to seize the greatest share of property, offices and mines.

This economic inequality and abuse of power turned into repression against their leaders, who were executed by hanging from the balconies of the Plazuela del Gato (Valentín Avicia). This conflict lasted a long time, and it seems important to stress that, in the feelings of the people of Potosí, there was never any room for neutrality or for giving up their rights. The massacres and lootings of Basques on November 6, 1623 could barely be attested, because the witnesses (children, women and Indians) feared deadly revenge. The skirmishes continued, and Corregidor (magistrate) Manrique was wounded by a bullet in his own home; because of this attack, both groups apparently reconciled in an act of agreement held in the Church of San Francisco.
The Game of Cachinas

Acts of violence and killings had broken out between the Basques and the criollos, on the one side because of the excess of abuses and privileges in the granting of mining claims and market stalls, the exploitation at work and the mistreatment, and because some grew rich while others grew poor. The complaints reached the ears of the Viceroy, the Marqués de Guadalcázar, who had on some occasion tried to talk with them and calm things down, with no result at all. This time he came up with a very different way for those two groups to face each other, a peaceful one, in which fathers, sons and whole families from both sides, Vicuñas and Basques, would take part: a very popular and challenging game, the game of cachinas (glass marbles). The active players would be the children of both groups, from the different mining districts. For this, prizes of great value would be offered, and the winners would pledge to put an end to these quarrels and differences.…

The game of cachinas is played with little glass spheres brought from ancient China, which each player kept in a chuspa (a small woven pouch). It requires a “table,” which is a completely flat stone belonging to the cobbled street, which the whole town enjoys in its entirety; the stones are river-rounded, and many of them shine in many colors in the sun’s rays because they are flecked with traces of pyrite, silver and gold. In this game both opponents must place on the table the PARADA, which is two or more cachinas, and then, both standing about five meters away, they throw and try to knock them off the table or get as close as possible. Whoever is closest has every right, if he can, to knock them all off and leave one for the end. Next he must give chase to the enemy, which is the opponent’s cachina. To do this the player has to crouch down and, with the thumb and the middle and index fingers of the right or left hand, flick the cachina to reach or touch the opponent’s. Many times the marbles are hidden in little caves or holes where they are placed on purpose, and it depends on the player’s skill or dexterity to reach them. If one misses, the other gives chase, and once he has touched it, his target must be what remains on the table; when he knocks it off, he is the winner, and that is how the bets go. In championships, only 12 cachinas are staked.

Among the prizes to be awarded, which were very tempting, so that surely nobody would want to miss this chance, the first was a chuspa of kidskin embroidered with gold and silver thread, holding 25 gold coins and 50 silver ones; the second was offered 5 gold and 20 silver; and the third received 15 silver coins and an alpaca poncho. Among the registered participants were the villas of Cantumarca, Miraflores, Caracoles, Munaypata, San Pedro and Pampa San Clemente, and the one chosen to stand for the Villa San Pedro was José Luis, the fourth child of Doña Catalina and Primo. He had been put forward by his uncle, the Maestro Rafael, who did work at the Corregidor’s hacienda. But before the event he had to compete against other contenders, and many doubted him because he was very small, in age and in height, compared with the other contenders, who had some Spanish or European descent. Happily he had no great trouble, eliminating them with the greatest ease, and you could see the joy and happiness in José Luis’s mischievous smile when he qualified. The joy and happiness spread to the grandparents, Abran and Martina, to his parents, Primo and Catalina, and to his brothers and sisters, Nelly, Jaime, Ricardo, José Luis, Charo, Evita, Jorge, Martha and Estequita, a large and very close family. All of them, in great jubilation, congratulated and kissed the winner, the grandparents proud of their children. And Ricardo, a counselor as always, told him: it is better that you go and rest and stay calm; tomorrow you must be very focused, and above all thinking about how you will face Pancho, who is one of the best of the group. It is only natural for a boy of that age to want to chase his dreams; he even begins to imagine what he wants to be when he grows up, and he works very hard to get what he wants, in this case to be champion. He gave all his free time to the game until the black mantle of night arrived, the very last moment, and so he sharpened his reflexes, his strength and his aim. His rivals criticized him a great deal for his age and his size, but he did not even listen to them; he ignored them and walked past whistling his favorite song, “Quisiera que volviera los días de mi infancia.” He was encouraged by his brothers, Ricardo and the eldest, who kept telling him: you know, brother, how to face your enemies and the public; you must not be afraid, for you everything is easy; breathe deeply, and when they look at you, look them straight in the face without lowering your head, and you will see that they will start to be afraid of you. And he would say: yes, little brother, just pretend you are playing with me, but mind you, I only give you chances, don’t forget that. José Luis, seeing his rascally face, would die laughing and say: oh, little brother, you and your illusions, you think you can beat me, that is impossible, it’s only a dream. Even so, he could not quite hide his nerves. Night came, bitterly cold, and every now and then he warmed his hands with his breath. When they got home, his sister Nelly, always attentive, was waiting with a lawita and some buñuelos with cane syrup, along with a cinnamon tea so hot that it gave off a thick steam that vanished at once, like a child’s breath. After finishing, completely satisfied, having received a soothing meal, and with no strength left at all, they went to their beds and fell into a deep sleep.

The appointed day arrived with a radiant sun and the energy of the mountains, as if foretelling that something good and dreamlike was going to happen, or as if it wanted to tell us that something had happened to its companion, the moon, which was slowly disappearing on the blue horizon. The field chosen for the contest was the little Plazuela del Mitayo, fitted out with stands that rose as high as the eaves of the roofs, which gleamed in their yellow and brown colors, and with balconies full of flowers set aside for the families who owned the most prestigious silver mills, where the authorities and the representatives of the two groups in conflict were seated. The night before, as if the weather wanted to help, a torrential rain had fallen and splendidly washed the fine cobblestones, leaving puddles of water here and there, through which slid threads and shapeless beads of mercury that marked out the playing table. This was a river stone, completely flat and level, like the tables made of Carrara marble belonging to King Charles V, which gleamed and stood out among the other rough rocks. These formed very special natural hiding places that looked like caverns, as if they had been made especially for an escape.

Suddenly the shrill blast of a bugle was heard, announcing, for all to see, the prizes to be competed for, which hung from Arabian horses, finely groomed and specially dressed, stepping very rhythmically to the beat of a drum: a large bag of kidskin embroidered with silver and gold thread, full of gold and silver coins, and other silver vessels holding silver and gold coins, all of them minted at the Mint, the historic building that was built by Indigenous and Black workers over a period of 20 years. Next, dressed in suitable clothes and attire, the participants or competitors came in and were cheered with frenzied applause. Then a deep, powerful, guttural voice was heard officially reading from a parchment the pledge and challenge of each one of them, steeped in pride and determination, and above all the duty to show gentlemanly conduct in this event, which was a true battle, and calling on the public to respect the players and both sides, wishing them, in the name of the Viceroy, good luck.

The organizer of the event formed two series of four teams each, in which the winning player would move on to the second and third rounds; whoever lost would compete no more, and the winner would go on. You could see great dedication and care in the players, and their supporters, full of intense emotion, cheered on their representatives. At moments it seemed that fights were about to break out that might even come to weapons: the Basques with their harsh tongue, and the Vicuñas with Castilian, Arabic and, most mischievous of all, Quechua, shouting, Cochiy- Cochiy Jáselo, khan ancha jatum kanki, dios ninchi yanapasunkha (you are very great, our God will help you); on the other side, rattles and castanets. And with that enthusiasm they reached the end of the matches, and the true finalists turned out to be a big lad named Francisco de Ortega and, most surprising of all, the brilliant José Luis, small in size but great in his character and his play, spurred on by the teasing shouts of Evita and Charo, who cried: go on, little brother, we are behind you, and we promise to make you the bread and jam you like best, go on, little brother! The contest began, and it was a real battle. The Basque started the game and with an accurate throw hit the paradas on the table. With an air of arrogance, Ortega, scorning the little José Luis, left on the table as his parada a violet cachina, as if he wanted to show his hatred and resentment toward those called blue-blooded. The next throw was one of retreat and escape, and so the duel began, with skill and with steely nerves. With a stealthy look, studying it from different angles, he tried to touch it, but unfortunately the missed shot landed two or three feet away, in a little cave, and a shout was heard saying that not even San Rafael could reach it. José Luis, with a calm and serene gaze, studied it from different angles; at times his look seemed that of a lynx or an eagle. He readied his delicate little wrist and his thumb and index finger, squeezing the crystal, sky-blue and red like a flame of fire, and launched it in an arc, and incredibly it made a sound as if a lightning bolt had struck a diamond, and the high-pitched shout was heard: I got you, I got you! He raised his arms to the sky as if giving thanks to the Lord on high, and then went on toward his target on the table, which lay very far away. The public was left speechless, in total silence, at the sight of such skill. Then it was Francisco’s turn to give chase, and in the end he did not manage it, because the clever José Luis cleared the table. And so the following matches went on, and they reached a tie in the number of games won, leaving the final. You could see how tired they were, but their spirits were high. The public, very nervous, did not know who would win; they shouted and cheered both opponents. Finally, in one of the moves chasing Francisco, José Luis was left with a very long shot, and you could see on his little face that he was in great pain: sadly, the nail of his thumb was broken and almost bleeding. Straining hard to bear the pain, he threw the cachina and managed to touch it, and finally he turned to the table and, with admirable skill, launched it like a rocket that flew to its target, knocking it off the table, and you could see and hear him: I won, I won! Crying and laughing at once, he was seen spinning around on the cobblestones without rhyme or reason. He was the champion, the champion! And the public roared: Joselin, you are a hero, an incredible boy, how did you do it? With this victory we have shown them that we are strong and persevering and that nobody can beat us. Congratulations, little one, you are a wonder! All the people, acquaintances, and above all those from the neighborhood, ran and shouted: we are the champions, nobody can beat us! Those on the other side, with sad faces, stood in a striking silence, not saying a single word; the unfortunate thing for them was that they had to stay on that stage for the awarding of the prizes, and one of those in charge was none other than the Viceroy, the Marqués de Guadalcázar, who appeared with other dignitaries. It was astonishing to see the public shouting with such emotion. The three champions appeared. The third prize was placed in the winner’s hands, to a shout; the second went to Francisco, who showed a certain displeasure, but once he felt the coins he calmed down. Finally, an astonishing cry: José Luis, José Luis, José Luis! The voices were so loud that they surely carried over the whole Villa. And to see the little boy so full of joy, he seemed to be seized by a spirit of happiness; he only laughed, and tears ran down his rosy cheeks. He cried and cried, all the more when they showed him the chuspa embroidered with silver and gold thread, into which they dropped, with a tin tin tin, the gold and silver coins, and hung it over his right shoulder. The Viceroy told him again and again: you are very brave and persevering; despite your age and your injured finger you have won the victory, which is a source of pride for your countrymen, your parents and your brothers and sisters, who feel very proud. Congratulations, congratulations…. In a voice broken between laughter and tears he repeated: thank you, thank you, thank you very much, sir, and thank you all. And once more the shout rang out like thunder: champion, champion, champion! At that moment he was showered with streamers and confetti, and amid this outpouring of joy he headed back to his beloved little plaza. Immediately the Corregidor summoned two representatives of the feuding groups to sign the pledge of non-aggression and peace; otherwise they would be punished and stripped of some of their contracts for mining claims and for the Rescate,

Jaime and Ricardo, the elder brothers, were very busy and could not be at the awarding of the prizes, which was considered the most important part, because they had set aside those days for some mining work and, above all, to go with their friends Alfredo Buhezo, Willy Varela and Walter Morales, who were devoted to searching for the traces, the trail left behind by the people close to the richest miner of all, Francisco Rocha. Rocha had always boasted of owning brilliants, jewels, diamonds and gold and silver coins, and many times he had promised the townspeople of the Villa that he would pave the streets with silver, just to obtain the rank of gentleman. This was one of their goals: to find, by any means, the TREASURE OF ROCHA. They would disappear for several days and turn up with pale faces, thinner than before, and for their parents this was a great worry. Every time they were asked, they said they had been in the Mondragón area, where Varela’s father had his fields of corn, broad beans and potatoes, which he took to town to sell and to eat. But that was only an excuse. As soon as day broke, their thoughts were centered and fixed on being in the area of the Devil’s Bridge, since according to rumor that was where one of the objects of their search was to be found. Others were drawn instead by the tapados, the hidden caches or chests that the Spaniards had stashed away when they left Potosí for a time, and who very often, for many reasons, never came back, so that their treasures were forgotten. These riches were the focus of attention not only for them but for many fortune hunters, just as it had been in the days of mining and silver. For them it was a way of improving their economic situation, which had always been a great worry for their parents. They saw with their own eyes how their parents earned their living with great sacrifice and risk, risk because of the work they did, and their pay did not justify the effort they made: they worked the whole day long in the mines, and their fortnightly wages were barely enough for food and a little clothing. Sometimes they repeated what they thought: education is good, but it does not answer our needs.

Speaking of the Devil’s Bridge, a place where the local people prayed as they crossed, especially as night fell, there surely came to mind one of the events that the old people of the area used to tell, and from which it takes its name, the result of a story that happened in this place.

So as not to take the wrong paths, as had often happened to them, the band of explorers would ask for the help of one of the farmhands, who knew even the most unimaginable corners of the region; they called him Albertico. And just as they reached the Devil’s Bridge, he would begin to tell one of the legends of the region, about the love of two young people. They say that on hearing these words the whole group would gather around him and pay attention as never before, far more than to their parents’ advice. He began, like all legends, by saying: there was a very handsome young peasant who fell in love with a very beautiful girl, the daughter of the corregidor, and they would meet in secret. But one day they were discovered by her father, who threatened him and laid down the following demand: if you love my daughter, you have to pay me her dowry, which is this amount of silver, within a year; otherwise you will never see her again. I am doing this because I have heard that you work hard and well, without forgetting what family you come from. The time starts from today. In this very short time the suitor promised to keep his word, and to do so he began to work at many things, as a miner, a helper, a carrier of ore. Up close he saw how the workers did their work facing many dangers, cave-ins, falls into mine shafts, and often being trapped in some of the workings; and most surprising of all, they ate almost nothing, they only chewed coca, which let them work without tiring. And on one of those afternoons he saw them bring out the remains of a miner killed in an accident, and heard the endless weeping of his little children and his wife, which truly stirred a deep sadness. After a year, having earned the dowry, on the day he was returning with what he had earned to fulfill his agreement with his sweetheart’s father, he set out with his donkey and came to a ravine that he had to cross. Suddenly the sky grew dark, as if foretelling a conflict. Thunder crashed along with lightning that lit up the whole place, and a torrential rain began, with the roar of waterfalls and the rumble of rolling rocks that numbed the senses. And he asked himself: what am I going to do now, how will I get to the town? It is impossible to cross. What can I do? Her father will not believe my word, and it will be his reason to forbid me to see her. In his despair an uncontrollable rage came over him; he kicked the rocks and pounded the edge of the gorge, weeping and shouting amid the lightning and the terrifying, unstoppable noise: what can I do now? I feel helpless and I have no hope left. And finally, into his confused mind, with no other choice or option, came the idea of asking the devil for help, and in a loud voice he said these words: [I would even hand over my soul if he would help me build a bridge. At that very instant, to his great astonishment, the devil appeared with a great crash and a certain smell of burning sulfur, and, standing before him, in a hoarse voice that grated on the ears, with an air of arrogance and self-assurance, having heard his request, he said: what do you want from me, why did you call me? You know that if I do it, it is on one condition: when I finish what you ask of me, I will take your soul. The young man told him his wish, to build a stone bridge, and without further ado he accepted on that condition: if it is finished by dawn, before the rooster crows, my soul will be yours. I agree, but keep it in mind,… before the rooster crows… A deal. In his extreme haste the devil cut the stones and set to work as if he were dozens of workers to build the bridge. The young man, calmer now and at peace, began to reflect and realized the mistake he had made, and he asked God for help: Lord, forgive me for this act. I did not know what to do in my hurry; my anxiety made me commit this madness. Please help this poor son of yours who is facing this calamity. And suddenly he perceived a sign, white like a radiance: the archangel Saint Gabriel. At that moment there was a clap of thunder and a flash of lightning, and he wondered: could this be the sign my Lord is giving me? At that moment he felt his body tremble, and an inner peace, no longer the despair that had gripped him. Suddenly there were signs on the horizon that dawn would soon arrive. He saw the devil hurrying to take the last stones to finish the edges of the bridge, and then, unexpectedly, many angels appeared who prevented the devil from lifting the stones and setting the last stage in place to complete it. And far away the shrill sound of the rooster’s first crow at dawn was heard. The demon, thwarted, spitting sparks and thunder, vanished into the infinite, saying: I will not forgive you.. In this way the young man saved his soul, and the bridge was left unfinished, but it no longer kept him from keeping his promise of the silver. And so his pledge was fulfilled, and the couple’s dream came true: the two young people married and lived happily for many years, with several children.
The Exploitation of Indigenous People in Colonial Times

After the genocide of the Indigenous peoples through the wars of conquest, the Spanish conquerors went on to impose a widespread enslavement of the Indigenous peoples. Many peoples did not submit to the Spaniards until they had been defeated militarily, and even among those who accepted Spanish rule, not a few ended up rising in revolt for many reasons, one of them being the merciless exploitation, and the diseases brought over and passed on by the conquerors. The Spaniards decided to stay, imposing a long-term state policy, and, more for economic reasons than out of any concern for human good, they adopted, in a derisory, insulting and degrading way, a policy of "protecting" the Indigenous people as free labor for the encomiendas, since land with no one to work it lost all its value, to the detriment of the encomenderos and of the Crown's tax interests.

1. The Spaniards used the labor of the Indigenous Americans in many kinds of work: as servants on their haciendas, as field hands, as helpers to the priests, and, hardest and most dangerous of all, in the mines. That work was assigned to young men, who stayed down there a long time, and if they did not die, they came out very sick or disabled. The Indians held in encomienda paid their tribute and worked on public works, building structures such as town halls (cabildos), jails, cathedrals and churches. The priests devoted themselves to instructing them in the Catholic faith, in groups known as Doctrinas. Many of these priests denounced the abuses to the Crown, such as Friar Montesinos and Friar Bartolomé de las Casas, who managed to reach the throne itself and lay this abuse before it.

The account of the Spaniard Reginaldo de Lizárraga, in 1605, says that the Cerro Rico of Potosí is like the center of the Indies. It is the wealth of the world, the terror of the Turks, the curb on the enemies of the faith and of the Spanish name, the astonishment of heretics, the silencing of barbarians; and nations such as Italy, France, Holland and Germany are rich thanks to this treasure, with the wealth that has come out of Potosí, and even the Turks keep in their treasury bars of gold carried from Potosí.

They work deep inside, in the shafts and rugged tunnels, where the darkness is perpetual and one cannot tell at all when it is day or when it is night. There is only a perpetual mist, and bitter cold too, and foul air alien to human nature. These were the conditions of the Indigenous people's hard labor.

The ore is extremely hard and has to be broken out with blows of an iron bar. Then they carry it up on their backs by a ladder made of three twisted strands of cowhide. A man climbs out carrying two arrobas, tied in a cloth across his chest with the ore it holds on his back. They climb three at a time; the one in front has a candle or small lamp tied to his thumb so that they can see, and so they climb a distance of about 300 meters, a horrible thing (as José Acosta relates in his account of the Indies of 1590). This exploitative labor, together with the military campaigns waged between rival factions, drained and diminished the labor force in the region, and it is here that the importation of enslaved Africans begins.

CONCERTAJE. - Another form of exploitation of the Indigenous people. It consisted of a contract between the cacique (chief) and the master whereby the mitayo Indian became the master's servant for a wage that was not equal to his work, in exchange for which the master fed him while he was in his service, until he died.

The years went by, and she became the inseparable companion of Doña Aurora, who taught her the whole practice of caring for the sick and attending births. Out of love and affection, Doña Aurora offered her surname to her as a daughter… and from then on she was called Martina Vidaurre de la Cruz. From that moment she felt very proud and immensely secure, no longer an orphan, though she never forgot her parents, who in spirit had set her on this path. The whole town admired her for her kindness, her help and, above all, her beauty. She cared with all her love for Señora Aurora during her illness, Martina came to regard her as her true mother; shortly afterward she died and left her entire estate to Martina. Martina carried on with the same work, always keeping the lady's respect and good manners… And so time passed, and she formed her family with Don Abrahán Ossio, a cabinetmaker and carpenter with many trades and occupations… They had met when he came to Señora Aurora's house to do carpentry repairs, over a long time, and in this way they formed a friendship that kept growing.
Mama Martina became a pillar of her community; her days and years passed among the sick, births, remedies, stories and tales of the past of great importance.

Whenever she spoke of it and told the story, she could not hold back her tears. It hurts me so much… every time I treated him I would hear the cries and screams of my son Jaime, the ñawilo, Cata's son. He had a wound on his leg and his arm that had appeared after a fall. I would wash it with herbs, and bits of his flesh and little pieces of bone would come out; I had to remove them until it bled, and then I applied a poultice they taught me long ago, called dragon's blood (sangre de drago), which comes from some palm trees of the tropics. I treated it every five days, and it stayed that way for a long time. And my heart would break when Antonito, still very small, crying, would shout at me: mamita, please, don't let him suffer, the pain is so great, for God's sake heal him… And so, after many years, he was healed by applying that poultice; and yet it left in all our minds a very sad and painful memory. In every one of Mama Martina's stories beats the strength of the earth and the memory of the valleys of Potosí.

Very often people arrived in the village asking where Doña Martina lived; usually they were seeking her care for someone's health. We need her urgently… She is not at home; the whole family has gone to Chagrahuasi, which lies south of the village. They are busy making furniture in the Villa of Viceroy Toledo, and Doña Martina is attending the women of the corregidor (magistrate) Don Ventura Santali, and of Quiroga, Ortega and Gambete, who are the owners, mercury refiners (azogueros); all her children are helping, Rafael, Catalina, Esther and Herminia… Go on, go on… And they did not know that the women asking for her were relatives of Don Félix Ortega, who were summoning her to Potosí, to the silver mill (ingenio) of Huayra; he was an azoguero, a producer of silver… They reached the place and spoke with Mama Martina. Please, Doña Martina, we beg you to come to Potosí. Don Félix is very ill, and the Spanish doctors have given him up for lost; they say they have exhausted every known form of treatment. Please come with us…

Such was the worry and the sense of responsibility that they called Don Félix's cousin, the surgeon Juan Ortega, well known and respected by those around him. On seeing and examining him, he ended by saying: there is nothing to be done. How could you have let him get into this state? Look, he can't even breathe… that anxiety, his mucous membranes completely purple, the great effort to breathe, a thoroughly toxic state. This illness is fatal; all you can do is pray and ask the Lord to protect him…. Hearing this, the family, deeply worried and in despair at seeing him in that state, almost dying, did not know what to do. Amid the voices and the weeping came the advice of one of their close comadres: to see and consult Doña Martina, the healer (curandera), who had great experience and who, above all, the neighbors said, had saved many lives. For God's sake, see him for me, do something to save him, we cannot bear this suffering any longer… weeping and weeping. Hearing this outcry, she knew it was an emergency. Without further delay Doña Martina heeded their pleas. She had not expected this from that family, but she had so great a spirit for helping, for being at the side of anyone who suffered pain, that she paid no heed to their class or origin, and she went in haste after putting her remedies in order, all of them made from herbs or animal fats. When they arrived at the silver mill, the great gate opened, and behind it a very young Black servant greeted them with a bow and led them down a corridor floored with finely worked brick blocks and lined on both sides by arches that reached as far as the door of the sick man's room. It was very spacious, adorned with very elegant furniture, and at the far end, in a very wide bed, he could be seen, attended by a girl whose head was covered in white and who wore a bib-apron. Doña Martina, deeply focused and calm, first of all observed and listened with great care: his posture, the labored breathing, the moaning, the drooling. Don Félix was completely unconscious; he did not respond to her greeting or to her questions, nor to the pressure she applied to the side of his shoulder. His skin had a marbled look, his eyes were deeply sunken and ringed with dark circles, his lips were purple and cracked, his breath putrid, and beneath his chin was a large swelling that reached down to the base of his neck, the skin taut, shiny and hard, very sweaty and hot, above all at the neck and throat. Please, I ask you, lay a straw mattress (payasa) and a soft phullu (woven blanket) on the floor and bring Don Félix down onto it, so that I can work better. She sent almost everyone out of the room, leaving only the sick man, and asked for a little ground quinoa, salt, egg, ground coca, honey and a cloth of vicuña wool. She began to pray while she prepared a poultice containing everything she had asked for. Over a brazier, in a small pot, she mixed the ingredients and warmed them over slow embers; it was dark green and sticky. She spread a layer a finger thick over the cloth and, taking it in her two skilled and gentle hands, applied it softly to the swollen part of his neck, with him sitting up. At that moment a terrifying scream of death was heard, one that set their ears ringing, and he fell backward onto the hides spread on the floor, expelling from his mouth a putrid, very foul-smelling mass of blood and pus, which was cleaned away at once. They laid him on his back with his head tilted back and turned to one side, and in that instant his bulging, congested eyes could be seen, giving the impression of a fatal end; and then a calmer, deeper breathing was heard. But Don Félix wore a different expression: a pale face, bluish lips; he did not respond to his wife's cries, he was completely limp, and it even seemed that he had died. Amid the weeping, the moaning and the cries of despair of the neighbors and of the mine workers of Doña Luciana, his wife, Doña Martina, with a word of encouragement that seemed almost magical, said aloud to everyone: stay calm, he is going to get well. How… it can't be… the best doctors have treated him without any result, and now it seems he is sleeping, he is breathing better, he is not agitated, we can see he is improving, this is a miracle, a miracle… All the onlookers heard this and were astonished, bewildered by this outcome. In the doorways and around the neighborhood there were murmurs of sorrow and resignation, because they did not believe in what she had done. Again, in a calm and commanding voice, she said: don't disturb him, and when he wakes up give him this preparation as a tea… and she withdrew… When the doctors learned that he was being treated by a midwife, they said: it cannot be, it is an insult; above all, she has overstepped their authority and deserves an exemplary punishment. They arrived on the scene, and worst of all, they had not been notified of what had happened; they were very angry to learn that he had been treated by someone else. They criticized and fumed, saying: how is it possible that, over our authority, you have brought in a healer who neither knows nor understands our art? We are the ones who know, and we cannot consent to or accept this. The wife listened to this protest, calmer now, and with a spirit of satisfaction and certainty she confronted them and made it clear: it is my decision, doctors, and I want no comments from you. I made that decision; she came at my pleading and insistence, nothing more. You doctors, in your meetings, urged me to resign myself, and said that your knowledge and wisdom had no answer, that there was nothing more you could do. You drew on your experience and wisdom, and it was exhausted. What could I do as a wife, facing such misfortune and sorrow?... The doctors were left perplexed, frozen and astonished by this answer…. Afterward Doña Martina, her face shining with spiritual happiness, silently and gratefully thanked her God for the help He had given and, above all, for guiding her with His holy hand. In silence she said to Him: a thousand thanks, a thousand thanks, my Lord, for giving health and life to this gentleman.

Doña Martina, completely renewed, her spirit strengthened and with greater drive, went to the Amoladera and Laca, mine tunnels belonging to the ladies Luisa and Petronila Vázquez, where she took an active part, at great risk, in the terrible epidemic of Intestinal Fever that broke out there, with signs and complaints of vomiting, fever, diarrhea, spasms and death within a short time. In this way it decimated the population of Potosí, especially the mining population, with the fatal consequence that work came to a standstill, and with it the supply of gold, silver and other minerals. So severe was this epidemic that of the 160,000 inhabitants the Imperial Town (Villa Imperial) of Potosí had at that time, 60,000 perished in the short space of the ten months that this scourge lasted. The plague was also marked by swelling of the feet up to the middle of the body; in others it appeared in the arms, the neck and the legs, above all in those who arrived on ships from Asia and Europe, and they died within a short time. The weakest could not endure a single day of suffering and pain, and the townspeople claimed it was a divine punishment… The so-called cholera was marked by continuous fever, repeated vomiting and abundant watery stools, which came again and again, up to 12 times, followed by spasms and cramps in the legs and arms, and then by screams that little by little fell silent until the sick lost consciousness. Their faces were pale, their eyes sunken, their skin wrinkled; they were utterly wasted, their lips dry, until they were completely exhausted and died soon after. The other group of patients had high fever, delirium, abdominal pain and nausea, most notably a yellowish color of the eyes and of the whole body; some vomited blood and passed dark, tarry stools, and the belly was very painful and rigid. Shortly afterward they raved incoherently, went into convulsions and soon died, many of them in the streets, in the mines, and others in the camps.

The faithful, gentlemen, mulattos, mestizos and Indians, talked about it; others wept and murmured in their native tongue: this is a divine punishment from the Pachamama; she is marking us with a punishment for our sins and the wrongs we do. The whole population organized a pilgrimage through the streets of the city. At the front went more than five thousand Indians in two rows, carrying very heavy crosses on their shoulders; with them went others from the confraternities and convents, who claimed that the only way to ask forgiveness for the sins and errors committed by themselves and the townspeople was to offer up this personal suffering and pain with prayers and weeping, and in that way they might win pardon from the punishment being dealt to them. They whipped their chests and backs with leather cords from whose ends hung nails and sharpened bits of iron, until they bled, enduring this martyrdom for the sake of others. Behind them followed some two thousand Spaniards, barefoot, their hands tied behind their backs and their heads covered in ashes, marching in two rows; in the middle came a hundred Spaniards, followed by the Franciscan fathers and the religious community that lived in Potosí, all carrying lit candles in their hands, and torches accompanying the Holy Christ of the True Cross (Vera Cruz). It is said that this was the only way the plague that was crushing the Villa Imperial could be stopped or brought under control. Because of these events, everyone's faith led them to the church, and that is why I want to tell you these stories and events of the past.
The Church of San Francisco

The Convent of San Francisco was one of the first temples where the Immaculate Host was adored, by the sons of the Seraphic Father, Father Morán, in the year 1547. The founder of the first church was General Pedro de Hinojosa, a conqueror of Peru and a captain of the rebel Pizarro. He later went over to the royalists, fought as a general against the Pizarrists, and was rewarded with the mine of Potosí, where he was appointed corregidor. He was later murdered in his home in 1553 by the followers of Sebastián Castilla. It was he who requested the presence of the Franciscan brothers in Potosí.

The church progressed quickly: in 1550 one of its wings was consecrated, and the first building was entirely finished in 1552. On March 15, 1626, the most productive silver mills were destroyed by an unexpected flood coming from a lagoon. A year later, in 1627, the Villa Imperial went through another of its worst catastrophes: the bursting of the San Ildefonso lagoon, which flooded the whole town with such force that countless Spaniards, parishioners and, of course, slaves and Indigenous people died; some were never found. More than 4,000 people are said to have died, and it destroyed many houses and buildings, among them the church of San

Francisco, above all the Small Cloister. Finding themselves in this situation, the friars were not seen for many days, and some said they had perished in the fury of the waters. They reappeared utterly haggard, with the look of deep dejection; they even lamented and wept, powerless in the face of that disaster. The damage was enormous. They did not know whether their tunnels and underground passages, built with great sacrifice and where many Indians and Black people had perished, were all flooded. After thinking and thinking, eager to restore it, they found themselves obliged to turn to many wealthy families to raise some funds. This news reached the ears of the richest miner in Potosí at the time, the maestre de campo (field marshal) Antonio López de Quiroga, who needed certain favors from the Church, since he sought a title of nobility that the Spanish Crown kept denying him, and he demanded and pressed this petition again and again. Quiroga agreed to give the friars the help they needed, on the request that he be recognized as founder of both the convent and the church, and on condition that he have a place in the crypts of the church where he and his family could be buried.

Years later Dr. Don Pedro Vásquez de Velasco laid the blessed cornerstone; the plan was to use all the material, and above all the stone blocks, of the church that had been brought down by the waters of San Ildefonso.

The flooding of the San Ildefonso lagoon was regarded as a divine punishment. Sadly, that rancor still ran in the veins of the factions of the Vascongados (Basques) and the Vicuñas, and the clashes began again. It was then that the Viceroy, the Marqués de Guadalcázar, who had been undecided until then because he did not know exactly who was in the right, decided to take matters in hand and somehow calm or pacify these social groups, set against each other in street battles and divided by economic and racial motives, which had bred such intense and lasting hatreds. He tried in some way to bring these two groups together peacefully, and with that aim he sought out their leaders and spoke with each of them, identified the causes and reasons for the conflict, and offered certain favors to both groups. They were left somewhat satisfied, though not persuaded out of the quarrels and hatreds so deeply rooted in them, but they agreed to keep a period of peace and harmony. To this end he called an event that would gather families, businesses, authorities and the townspeople in general to take part in one of the most popular games, played above all in the neighborhoods and by every social class, which had been brought over from the poor quarters of Spain: the game of cachinas (glass marbles). On April 29, 1625, at last one could perceive and feel that peace reigned among those who remained of the Vicuñas and Vascongados, who went back to their mills to work and to extract silver and tin (information taken from the book by Edgardo Caballero and Berna Hausberger).
The Holy Christ of the True Cross

One Friday morning in the year 1550, at the entrance doors of the Church of San Francisco, the Franciscan Fathers found a cedar box in the shape of a cross. They opened it at once, and inside it was… the venerated effigy of the Lord of the Holy True Cross (Vera Cruz). It was believed then that angels had carried the box there and that the image was the work of heavenly spirits.
As the years went by, a certain Martínez y Vela, in his history of the Villa Imperial, refers to the following.

The presence of the Lord of the Holy True Cross, found in the cedar box, created a very serious legal conflict over who owned it, involving the trustees Don Melchor de Escobedo, Don Ramón de Trujillo and Don Alonso de Rodríguez, and a lawsuit with the priests of the Mother Church (Iglesia Matriz), who wished to move the image to their own church. Once they even tried, and got halfway, and to everyone's surprise the next day it reappeared at the doors of the Church of San Francisco. Finally a council was formed with the confraternities, stewards and notaries to decide where it should stay, and then Viceroy Toledo stepped in and settled the matter with an ordinance.
