Although he had been a skeptic, he changed abruptly the moment he saw that miraculous image, whose fame had spread throughout Peru and even further: it was a divine gift, a holy relic, which no one should meddle with. He believed in its miracles, and therefore it was to be enthroned in the Church of San Francisco.

All these events overwhelmed his superstitious spirit and filled Viceroy Toledo with wonder: its face, its hair and beard were splendid, natural-looking; he had felt their warmth and softness when he pressed his face and his lips to it, and it left him with a sense of peace and humility. This is the account that was sent to Dña. Leonor Fernández de CORDOVA, an Andalusian lady who lived in Potosí.

Martínez y Vela tells us, with great respect, that sinners tremble before that image, the wicked repent through a supernatural force, and the unfortunate who pray to it find relief from their sorrows. The Reverend Franciscan Fathers relate that they make relics from the hair and beard of the Holy Christ; once they cut off part of the beard, and miraculously it grew back. The legend adds that every year on Holy Thursday, after the procession, the Franciscan Fathers comb its hair, eagerly gather the loose strands, and then hand them out as relics to all the faithful, so that they may be protected against every evil.

This crucifix, venerated under the devotion of the Holy Christ of the True Cross of Potosí, began to gain so many devotees, and its miracles were so frequent, that they astonished locals and strangers alike. And so, according to tradition, Viceroy Toledo had a sworn report of these events drawn up, which he deposited in the archives of the Franciscan monastery…
The Cárcamos, or Silver Mills

The techniques for obtaining silver in colonial times were very rudimentary, since those who exploited the silver wealth did so in a precarious way. The method they used, moreover, was not very effective.

At first, as we mentioned, the Spaniards used the method of smelting in clay furnaces. The ore was extracted and then smelted into ingots. Not much was gained from the ores, and burning firewood and yareta, a wild plant of the high plateau, made it laborious work with little profit.

Later, in the sixteenth century, an Aztec who worked with a Sevillian miner, Bartolomé de Medina, brought the amalgamation or patio method. It consisted of grinding the ore, spreading it out in the patio and sprinkling it with mercury, which has a strong affinity for gold and silver. This was a true revolution in American silver mining. The basis of this process was the use of mercury, or quicksilver (azogue), which was mixed with the ground silver ore and left for a few months in great patios such as Huayra. Then this mixture, or amalgam, was washed and smelted, yielding purer silver, and afterward part of the mercury was recovered to be used again. The smelting of this mixture was done by Indigenous people or Black slaves, using furnaces fueled with llama dung and yareta brought from the plateaus, all of it supervised and controlled by very harsh overseers. Huayra had some twenty ore depots and stables for the mules that hauled the loads, and a cascade of spring water built of finely carved stones stacked to a height of 50 feet, from which, with a spectacular roar, they washed the ground ore in the sieves, where the precious metal was sorted out, to then go on to be dried and smelted.

The cárcamos are the structures of the amalgamation mills, the silver mills (ingenios) of the mercury refiners (azogueros). They were the places where the extracted ore was concentrated or processed, and they also had pits for depositing or storing it. They were generally built along the riverbank, like the well-known Huayra and the other one, the Rivera de Vera in Cantumarca. Besides these works, the ore was crushed to allow greater contact with the mercury, that is, amalgamation, which was the technique used to process the tons of silver that made the European countries rich. (drawing).

The cárcamos were true walls and bridges that crossed lands and rivers, built with the sweat and toil of Indians and slaves, who used their backs and hands as their only tools to haul the massive rocks from the quarries and to mix the earth and lime. Then, under the direction of an overseer, they piled it all up, from the foundations to the channels, which reached a height of 8 to 10 meters. Along these the water flowed until it reached the rudimentary metal screens, where the metals were washed and sorted before entering the amalgamation process.
The Imperial Town of Potosí

For those who do not know, it is very important to tell that on the 1st of April, 1545, King Charles V, Emperor of Germany, declared in the name of Spain, and of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and said in a hoarse, faltering voice: we take Possession of the Mountain, silent as it was, naming the first mine La Descubridora, or Pailaviri, it being the first material wealth to be settled in the service of God our Lord and for the benefit of His Imperial Majesty. And so the Imperial Town (Villa Imperial) of Potosí was founded. This extraordinary mountain stands 5,183 meters above sea level, and its circumference is one league, that is, a circuit of 25,563 feet. Its summit resembled a perfect cone, displaying on its flanks numerous spoil heaps of many colors and shapes, where they work the mine mouths through which the riches of silver, gold and other hidden minerals are extracted and obtained.

At the foot of this novel peak of the Andes, where a river passed, houses were built for the miners, as if by commission. Later, with the arrival of Viceroy Toledo, work began on the Mint, the churches and other buildings, and the town was definitively founded, and recorded in documents, under the name of VILLA IMPERIAL DE POTOSÍ. Seeing how the population was growing through migrants and the native birth rate, by order of Viceroy Francisco Toledo himself, the hydraulic engineers were commanded to build the lagoons of Kari Kari, five in number, using Indians and some Black slaves as laborers. At first the lagoons were waterproofed with cowhides. The water was essential for washing and separating the metal in screens made for that purpose.

At the beginning of the eighteenth century the Villa Imperial of Potosí boasted a hundred thousand souls and many organizations based on mining. Indeed, mining gave the Basques great economic and political power. They were made up of just 80 families, and they took possession of a great number of mines and silver mills, which was creating a monopoly, while at the same time abuses of power were brewing, and ever sharper social tensions arose with the common people in the streets. These economic interests and power struggles reached unbearable extremes, leading to a brazen greed for what they coveted. It meant not only growth in population but also, naturally, attracted every kind of luxury, custom and product, which, according to the Jesuit Father Acosta, could satisfy any conceivable desire in abundance. Potosí certainly had everything: 14 dance schools, 4 fencing academies, 36 gambling houses and 400 recognized brothels, and it also had so many churches per square meter; religion was the foundation for easing consciences and forgetting the guilt that the riches dragged along with them.

The world's ambition grew as word of so much wealth spread, and a migrant population arose such as had never been seen before in Europe or America. From 170 Spaniards and 3,000 Indigenous people, within 2 years 2,500 houses had been built, housing 14,000 people. After the census ordered by the Viceroy, it was reported that the population growth could not be controlled, reaching as many as 160,000 citizens in the Villa Imperial, of whom 6,000 were Black people, mulattoes and zambos of both sexes. Among those identified were merchants, hustlers, miners, fortune hunters and thieves who settled there. Most of the Black people worked for their masters on the mountain or in domestic labor; the more servants a master had under his command, the greater the symbol of social ostentation. This gave rise to different ways of life, cultures, social economies and religions, which set them apart not only in these respects but also in their burials: Spaniards, priests and their kind were buried in the churches or the grounds around them, while Indians, Africans and Moors were buried near their own neighborhoods, because it was doubted whether they had souls at all; the others, meanwhile, were close to heaven, or else bought themselves a place or plot at the moment of their death.

Potosí truly is one of the great wonders of the world. People lived surrounded by silver, wealth, luxury, ostentation and power. The main square displayed swords brought from Toledo, glass from Venice, linens from Holland, ivory from Africa; there were 36 gambling houses, festivals and bullfights. Along these lines, because of the economic interests and the other factors mentioned above, two very opposed and rebellious social groups arose, as we pointed out earlier, shaped by their backgrounds, influence, origins and so on. On one side were the Vicuñas, recognizable by their hats made of vicuña skin, made up of Indigenous people, mitayos, Andalusians, Castilians and Criollos devoted to work in the mines; on the other, the Vascongados, also called Vizcaínos, of Basque origin and from Burgos in Spain, who seized economic and political power by holding prominent administrative posts, and only they were allowed to stand in elections for the mayoralties and other representative offices. They also took over the richest veins of the mountain and the mercury refiners' mills for producing silver (by the process called amalgamation) between the years
The Royal Mint

Because there was such brisk trade in clothing, jewelry, furniture, and petacas or strongboxes of leather and fine wood in the shops and markets of the City of Potosí, and above all in the sale of silver, tin and gold, the coins produced in Peru and Argentina were not enough to meet the demand. That is the reason for the creation of the new Royal Mint (Casa Real de Moneda), devoted to producing these coins in sufficient quantity for the dealings and commerce of these kingdoms. According to Burzuo, by higher orders of Viceroy Francisco de Toledo, Potosí, that Mecca, was given the honor of being the new site for building the Royal Mint, under the responsibility of the Potosí master builder Jerónimo de Leto, and it was set up in the Plaza del Gato on the 8th of November, between the end of 1575 and 1595 *; it took twenty years to complete, at a total cost of $1,148,453.6 reales, and it occupied an area of two city blocks, built of lime and dressed ashlar stone and cedar wood brought from the borderlands of Chuquisaca and the Valleys of the Pilcomayo. When it was finished, the King of Spain remarked, in view of the cost of the work, that the building must be made of silver, as Don Alejandro Garland relates in his work Los medios circulantes usados en el Perú (The Currencies Used in Peru).
The Mint consists of five inner courtyards and nearly two hundred rooms, laid out and arranged across its almost 8,000 square meters, figures that show the tremendous majesty of this building.
In the entrance courtyard a majestic mask of the god Bacchus stands out. It smiles sarcastically, with an ironic grimace aimed at the Spaniards, as if bidding them to leave the region.

With the trade in Black slaves, the individual became an object of exchange, a piece of merchandise or a working machine. The Spaniards who came in search of fortune brought their African slaves with them to do domestic work or to join their adventures of conquest. Quite different, and much harsher, was the situation of the Black people used as labor in the Mint. They were the fundamental basis of the local and regional economy, working in the worst human conditions, treated like true beasts without souls, facing the harsh weather and intense cold at more than 4,000 meters above sea level. The slaves spent years at the furnaces. The Black man was considered a slave, a living dead man or a ghost, cut off from his land, his customs and his culture. And so he became a hostile and embittered being, because of the hard work he did and the treatment he received at the furnaces of the Mint. (Historical Archive of the Casa de Moneda)
The first workshops for minting and die-stamping gold and silver coins for circulation were set up by Don José Fernández de Córdova and Don Calixto Moreira (Crónicas Potosinas).

Potosí minted legal coinage from 1574. A first record testifies that 26,531 pesos were coined between the 28th of March, 1574 and the 7th of December, 1575, with one real of seigniorage paid per mark of silver.

The coins that were minted would serve to pay the day laborers, Indians, Criollos and Portuguese, who made up the workforce, and they were marked for use within the Río de la Plata and the Spanish Crown.

The Mint had 12 Black slaves in good physical condition, who worked at the three furnaces that were set up under the charge of the foremen, or furnace masters, Pedro Real, Lucas Martín and Pedro Salazar, each responsible for four slaves. Ref. Crónicas Potosinas, Volume I – Documento histórico Casa de Moneda Potosí – José A. Fuentes.

In those days an unusual bustle could be seen in Potosí, with the arrival of many workers seeking jobs in the new silver and tin mine mouths, while those who had taken part in building the Mint wished to carry on with their labors as mitayos.
A Wedding in the Conventillo

One sunny afternoon, under a sky so completely blue it was as if a painter had laid his brush on it, reaching down to the mountains in a whitish tint, the temperature pleasant and the pure air you breathed awakening a feeling of freedom and joy, so very contagious, a group of country folk appeared at Doña Martina's house carrying bundles on their backs. They asked her to forgive them for surprising her, and speaking in their almost sung Quechua, they said: we bring you these gifts with all our love and respect, to invite you to our village and to ask you (mañakarle) to be the godmother of the casanaku, or wedding, of Anselmo… that is why we brought you this present; if you accept, it will be a pride and an honor for us that you receive it…. Their bundles held all sorts of food: chicken, goat cheeses, corn on the cob, wine, and many kinds of fruit, like grapes, quinces, figs, peaches, pears…. Along with a jug of aloja, a very sweet and pleasant corn drink.

Now tell me, who is Anselmo's bride…. You know her, ma'am, it's Marcela, Jacinta's daughter. Of course, how could I not know her, I was the one who looked after her from the day she was born. She's a good girl, and what can I say about her beauty, and so hardworking, always helping her mama. How lovely, I am all for it and very happy. Everyone there helped themselves and enjoyed all the food and fruit they had brought… Every now and then Agustín would say to her again: Godmother, your presence makes us very happy, and above all the people of the community respect you very much. I'm going to play for you on my charanguita and sing what you like best, that song… pistola en mano, arbolito en miniatura…. Cotagaiteñita… this Agus never gets tired of talking… yes, Dña. Martina… we're done now, we'll be waiting for you at the barn (galpón) on the appointed day. Very well, I will be there with your godfather Abrahán. Yes, Godmother, we'll be waiting for you….

The days went by, and she had the gifts ready: two lambs, a set of plates, spoons and three phullus woven of multicolored wool. The two of them dressed in their best clothes and bright shawls, and when they arrived at the barn they saw many guests, all with their gifts, and it surprised her to hear most of them greeting her and shouting Godmother. Godmother, how wonderful that you're at this celebration… most of them applauded her…. What a feeling of joy it stirred in Don Abrahán's head… Martina, how well they know you and respect you. Not just me, they do it for you too. Yes, really… come on… come on. I just saw the tata cura (the priest) go in, we mustn't be late, we have to be there…. As was fitting, the bride and groom were already at the front, and we had to take our places beside them… The couple, Anselmo and Marcela, smiling, in clothes that stood out for their color and whiteness, a bright pollera and blouse, in step with the happiness that showed on their faces, as if both were bound for heaven, so that no one could ever part them. The priest began by saying: are you sure you want to become a couple and have children, for good? Both, almost shouting: yes, tatay. Will you look after and care for each other when one or the other is sick… yes…. Will you work and earn a little money for your little house, your children and for times of sickness? Yes. Will you respect each other at all times? Yes. Do you swear that you will never separate… yes. Whatever problem you have, call your godparents, and they will advise you or punish whichever of you is to blame. Yes. Before me and our God and your godparents, I declare you Husband and Wife. I place these silver bracelets on you both… give each other a big hug and a kiss…. Applaud the new couple… I bless you, and may you be happy…… The godparents and guests threw misturas (confetti), little wildflowers and colored candies, surrounding the new couple, may you be very happy, they shouted. Soon after the gifts arrived: sheep, goats, pots, llama hides, blankets, hats, ponchos, plates, pots, ladles, jugs of chicha, etc., etc.… let them dance... let them dance, you could hear, like a chorus.

Coming back home, a little tired, to my great surprise I see and hear people crowded together and a tune of music. I see people and musicians in new, brightly colored clothes, with misturas and streamers, and silver jewelry pinned to their shawls and hanging from their ears, flashing like lightning, as they followed along with their rhythmic movements behind a bride and groom. The bride was very beautiful, and the groom, to my surprise, was maestro Anselmo, the watchmaker, who in spite of his limp kept the rhythm, and you could see the joy on his face. Accompanying the band was grandpa Agapito, grandpa Abrahán's brother, with his organ, which he played with astonishing agility and skill. But there behind, I see Uncle Rafael, with his hands and some thin little sticks, playing drums and bass drums, happy as can be. Only now do I understand why he flew out of the house all dressed up,, and everyone there showed a very contagious joy. At the other end you could hear a very melodious voice and lyrics that portrayed the people around him. It was none other than the sturdy young man, holding his guitar slung from his shoulder, Luis Rico, the Tupizeño from the South, as they called him… He sang this song, dedicating it to the bride and groom, the godparents and the guests: with all my love for you all.

lines: El conventillo se ha vestido de amarillo
Adornado con retamas y con cintas de papel.
Aquí en el patio se ha instalado una gran mesa
Bien tendido Dña. Martina la madrina de Anselmo
De los balcones cuelgan globos, serpentinas
Elegante la madrina con manta de alpaca y vicuña
Ahí en la esquina preparada la banda con trompeta,
Batería, un violín bajo trombón
Llegan los novios con los padres y padrinos
Y contentos los vecinos han formado un callejón
Vuelan arroces, serpentinas y misturas y las niñas
Que dulzura que de blanco son un primor

Hacen sándwich de chola, elegantes las charolas
Con las copas de champagne

Dña. Martina y Don. Abrahán los padrinos
Que a pesar de su dolor nunca pierden el compas
Y la costumbre como lo hacían antes
Ya los novios elegantes se vienen bailando el vals.
La la………….

blocks.text: When this song ended, there was joy all around, and above all the tears of the bride and groom and of the godmothers, which were nothing but the expression of what everyone at the party felt, and a loud round of applause rose from all who were there. Then a young waiter came by with a tray holding countless little glasses of many colors, and he went up to each of the dancers, who helped themselves eagerly, wishing the newlyweds eternal happiness and that the little ones to come would be their hope and their reason for living… The party went on, and more and more guests kept arriving with many gifts, some with a pair of goats and others with a finely decorated llama. Each time such a gift arrived there was applause, and the band struck up a special rhythm with a very joyful tune. But what was surprising was that the most honored guest of all was Mama Martina. People greeted her with such respect and told her, Mama, you have to be the godmother of my children, because you will bring them great luck and you will also set them on the path of being hardworking and good. Hearing these words, I felt very proud, and at times I felt like shedding a few tears for my lovely grandmother, who never told us who her parents were or what they were like, or how she came to this land. She would say, I am from the valley called Cotagaita, where everything is joy, and the same goes for work. What work her parents did, everything was left half told. The only thing she narrated in full were the carnival festivities (carnestolendas), when people worked for a whole season just to spend what they earned on this fiesta: clothes, food and the chicha they made. She used to say that nothing had ever made her so happy. But the surprising thing was that she never spoke of her sufferings. She was very brave; she was never sad, and she always had a penetrating gaze, full of the will to win and keep going.

Unexpectedly, Doña Luciana appeared, the wife of Don Félix Ventura, owner of the Huayra silver mill (ingenio), where silver and gold were refined with mercury… She came up very respectfully and said, I found out from one of my workers that you, Doña Martina, were the godmother, and I could not stay away from this occasion, I who owe you so much and will never be able to repay the great favor you did me by saving my husband, and I can confirm that everyone knows you and respects you, more than they do me. Martina answered her, Don't worry, it is important to be at their side; I come to them when they need me, they call me when they are sick or when they need advice… What joy and satisfaction it gives me to hear that, Doña Martina; it comes to me as a recommendation and advice too, and I am very grateful to you… Doña Martina, to keep the joy going I have brought you some lads and a young man who has just arrived from my home region of Valencia, and they will sing you some songs that hold their memories and inspiration… Let me introduce them: they are Milton Cortez and Willy Claure, from the Chaco of your homeland, very well-mannered young men… A pleasure to meet you, Doña Martina, everyone talks about you. And we want to dedicate this song to the bride and groom and, above all, to your esteemed self… It is called…

lines: C A N T A R I N A
Desde que me vi en tus ojos
Voy de desvelo en desvelo
Con la ilusión de que un día
quieras llevarme a tu cielo
por besar tus labios rojos
por ser parte de tu aliento
dejaría todo, todo porque vengas
a mi encuentro...
desde que cantas mi nombre
cuando me nombra tu boca
voy lloviéndome en tu cuerpo
mientras persigo tu sombra
si la suerte me acompaña
y tu corazón me abriga
viviría abrazado a tus encantos...
vida mía déjame besarte el alma
regalarte mil mañanas bañadas
del canto y el Rosio de mi vos
ven a fundirte a mis brazos
ven a calmar mi dolor
La ra la ra la ra.
blocks.note: "Cantarina," a love song the young musicians dedicate to the newlyweds and to Doña Martina (kept in the original Spanish).

blocks.text: What joy and emotion showed in the guests, with their applause and tears. More, more! they cried, what a melody, what verses! And so the party went on until the small hours of the night, as they enjoyed the drinks and the dancing. The time has come for us to leave, tomorrow we have a lot of work, said Doña Martina and Abrahán, taking their leave of all the guests with the greatest respect, amid a thunder of applause and gratitude for their presence….

I remember that early that morning I had promised to go to my uncle Rafael's workshop. He had a job for me, and I showed up faithfully. The work waiting for me was to finish sanding and varnishing some frames that master Nico had ordered. Uncle Rafael told me, if you want to eat, I'm leaving you some quinoa pisara and a little goat cheese, and a little coca tea; help yourself, I have an engagement and I can't miss it… He left in a hurry and didn't say where. I set about sanding the frames very carefully. They were carved in high relief, and I think they had taken him many days. They were of mara wood, and you could see the fineness with which the gouges had been passed over the whole surface, which I had to smooth without losing the angles and edges of the floral work. I wondered how he did it, so I went looking for the chisels and gouges and took a piece of wood with the same grain as the frames. The first thing I did was draw a rose with its branches and other details. I set the gouges along the edges of the drawing, but I couldn't make a cut; it was very difficult for me. Then I noticed some of my uncle's unfinished pieces, which had vertical cuts, and that lesson showed me that the first thing I had to do was outline the drawing, holding the chisel upright and tapping gently all around the contour. In that way I achieved what I was after, which was to get into the wood, and even so I could barely raise a shaving, because I was using the wrong gouge, completely blunt. I took another one, and with what joy and satisfaction I watched it run and lift the shaving in a spiral! I went on and on patiently until I had cut the whole outline of the rose. Next I did the petals, with such ease, and I enjoyed it; then the stem. I said to myself, no wonder my uncle carves so often, because you forget about time and everything else… Then I came to and asked myself what I was doing… I remembered that I had to finish sanding and begin varnishing. I went back to the earlier job: the sanding still had to be finished, and the glue and the varnish prepared. The varnish had to be applied gently over the whole surface of the frames, then left to dry, and afterwards rubbed little by little until it shone. And so I did, spending the whole morning on it, but I was very satisfied.

One afternoon, on the 22nd of May, the cold wind was blowing down from the summit and the slopes of the mountain. You could hear it whistling as it bent the paja brava under the force of that air, and so it reached into the depths of one's soul and bones, leaving hands and face so cold that they brought on a feeling of weariness and sleep. We walked a good stretch and found Nelly at home, very worried about the risks Mama Martina faced with the many sick people she tended, and wishing she would come home as soon as possible. With those thoughts, her hands took up the dough to fry some buñuelos, and she was also making an api of purple corn. At that moment my brothers Jaime, Ricardo and José Luis appeared… Nelly gave a shout that startled them… Antoñito, I made you what you like best, buñuelos, little brother. Today is your birthday, did you forget? Yes… sister, I was busy helping Don Juan, I have to sand some table legs, my arms are sore and I'm very tired. In any case, I thank you with all my heart, sister, you are always mindful of my days and my dreams, I don't know how I can ever repay your help. Once again, my gratitude. Before I forget, Antoñito, uncle Rafael came looking for you to help him; he wants you to visit him at his workshop first thing tomorrow. He was very happy to hear this message; it always brought him something new, an extra job, a task, or a hope, and he was always willing. Thinking and thinking, he went to his bedding on the floor, lay down completely worn out, closed his eyelids and covered himself with the phullus woven of llama wool, falling into a deep sleep from the weariness of the day.

In his dream, which seemed like reality, he could be seen walking in a great hurry and climbing onto one of the mules of the pack train, which was bound for a very distant destination along far-off roads. He was dressed in very special little clothes: a little vest and a little woolen poncho, white trousers and a little cap with a very prominent tassel, and the whole family was seeing him off: Antoñito, Antoñito. Yanita, may all go well for you, you are going so far away, we hope you come back soon, and I hope you bring news, she said, weeping. Don't cry, he kept repeating, I promise to come back well trained and responsible, he answered, and he too wept in silence, showing his great pain, that pain so intense that every fiber of feeling breaks, because one is parting from those who gave one life and endowed one with every quality, skill, respect and responsibility, and above all with the strength to face the dangers and challenges of life without faltering; and parting too from the brothers and sisters with whom one shared, day and night, joys and sorrows. And now, on this occasion, he was leaving his home without knowing what fate held for him in a faraway place, longing urgently to fulfill his wish to be a carpenter and carver, a painter and a doctor… In the other world, unknown to his eyes, as if his mind could command space, in a very short time, like a flash of lightning, he moved from one place to another, coming to know incredible places and, above all, people: masters who handed him their secrets so that he could carry out certain important tasks, such as curing certain illnesses with plants and minerals. They showed him how, working at the bedside of the gravely ill, who, surprisingly, showed a miraculous recovery on receiving these preparations. Suddenly he found himself in a colorful setting, with gentlemen who looked like monks standing before canvases, holding brushes and boards covered with a multitude of many-colored paints. Facing him were gentlemen with whitish beards, who spoke to him naturally and told him: you must prepare these ochres, panels and cloths, but you must also carry on with your work and your paintings in this same order and technique, and above all you must do it with great love and dedication, transporting yourself in your mind to the very place, as if you were living or feeling those impressions or joys. This craft requires a commitment of mind and body; otherwise it has no value or meaning, if you do not follow these rules. To be a good painter….

He woke with a start, very agitated, his heart pounding, amazed at everything that had happened in his dream. What had happened to him seemed to foretell the paths he would have to travel in his life at the cost of intense sacrifice, but he was not afraid of it and was ready to achieve it no matter what. Then it came back to him, and he remembered that he had an engagement with his uncle Rafael at his workshop, and without losing
The Story of Don Francisco Paula Sáenz and María

Wake up, wake up, sleepyheads! It was the voice of my sister Nelly. Have your breakfast, we have buñuelos and a tojori that will set you up well for today's work. But first I want to tell you a story that Doña Lalica from the general store told me yesterday, and it happened some years ago. It is about Don Francisco Paula Sáenz. They say he was the son of King Charles III and an Italian princess, whom the King courted in secret; she was very young and beautiful. So that the King's wife would not find out, and to avoid family gossip, they sent his offspring to our land of Potosí with the post of governor, or intendant. When he arrived, he was astonished at the great wealth of the Imperial Town (Villa Imperial) of Potosí. Days and weeks went by. One cold afternoon, with only a few rays of sun, on the street where gentlemen and young men of different origins, generally well-to-do miners or merchants, went to stroll and converse, the so-called Boulevard, a narrow street where one could admire modern, luxurious, many-colored clothes and jewels hanging from the ears, matched with brooches of gold and silver, there stood out among them a very slender, young and enchanting woman, on the arm of an elderly gentleman who was very fortunate for it, and above all for the respect the passersby showed him. People also said he was the owner of the mines of Porco and that he was her father; and sadly they whispered that he kept her in complete isolation. She had everything, but her beautiful face showed loneliness. She devoted herself to household tasks, and her extreme beauty stood out all the more with the gowns and ornaments she wore. Since she had awakened great interest and attraction in him, he found out more and questioned the neighbors, and they confirmed that the man was not her father: he had abducted her from Peru, a descendant of Inca royalty, when she was barely 7 years old. The culprit, who passed himself off as Portuguese, was none other than a Jew named Jacobo Moses. And so the lovely María grew up displaying all her splendor and monumental beauty, and so it was that by chance she met the intendant, Don Francisco, on one of her strolls. They had barely looked at each other when the prince noticed María's beautiful eyes, black and with a sweet gaze, which sent out radiant waves of attraction that made his heart race, beating so hard that it seemed to choke him. The two of them looked at each other and, seconds later, as if by a magic spell or an irresistible harmony, they were drawn together like two poles and ran at the same moment into an embrace so intense, fed by the fire of burning love. But then they pulled apart forcefully, as though it were an imminent and immense sin or danger.

Many days passed without their seeing each other, but both dreamed day and night of the hour and the day of their next meeting. So the weeks went by, and in secret, in out-of-the-way places, they met and declared their love. And in a soft, whispering voice María said: To love you as I love you is the supreme happiness that cannot be enjoyed here on earth; it is to live for you alone.... And Don Francisco answered her: To love you as I love you is to have no thought but yours, which thinks of me, no heart but yours, which devotes all its beats to me, all its fervent love; to love you as I love you, daughter of a King. So time passed, and both gave their souls and their bodies entirely, with a sincere and pure love. A secret, as they considered it, that was quite impossible to hide; many times their souls had such strength that they could not control them. On one of those many occasions they were seen by people who marveled and whispered among themselves: what will Don Jacobo say if it reaches his ears? He kept her like a jewel so precious that he allowed no one to come near her or to call at his house on any pretext.

When Jacobo Moses learned of María's love affair through the talk and gossip of the neighborhood, and saw besides her indifference and her behavior, he fell into a deep depression. He did not know how to act, until one day he reacted, saying: Oh, I will kill that wretch, and she will die too! He could not carry out his wish; he looked very worn out and unable to go on living with so much suffering. At night María seemed to hear weeping and sobbing, and in his sleep he repeated: no, no, please don't take her from me, she is my life, and without her I will die, she is my breath. A short while later, as usually happens to those who suffer repeated frustrations, such as those marked by the impossible love of a beautiful young woman, he was found, very haggard, hanging lifeless from a rope from one of the beams of his house. So ended the life of Don Jacobo, with riches but without love, which cannot be bought. Feelings such as love, the force of life, are impossible to obtain even with all the wealth in the world.

Years later it became known that they had married and had a son, who was abducted on the orders of the authorities of the town and handed over to the Indigenous group of the Jucumaris, where he was raised and grew up like the natives and was called Juan, or Huallpa Rimachi. The legend tells us that he was the son of Governor Francisco Paola Sáenz and of María Sawaraura, the Indigenous princess who was abducted by Jacobo at the age of 7. He is known as the guerrilla poet; he was born on June 24, 1793, and died in 1814. Later it was learned that he had been one of the guerrilla fighters of Manuel Ascencio Padilla and Juana Azurduy de Padilla, who were his adoptive parents…
The Wise Master of Painting

The next day, at dawn, Antoñito, with his usual smile, a little boy of about 9, dark-skinned, with a lively gaze, very large black eyes, dark and slightly wavy hair, slim build, nimble in whatever he did, and above all ready to answer any question or to ask about his doubts, remembered that he had an engagement with his uncle Rafael. He got his clothes ready, drank the api his sister had made him, and ran off to his destination. He appeared knocking at the gate and greeting him: good morning, uncle Rafael, you're working hard. Yes, son, how good that you came. I want you to help me sand and varnish these picture frames, and these two coffins; they are needed urgently. The frames are for the works of Don Melchor Pérez de Holguín and Nicolás Cruz, for the Church of San Francisco. This little job, as you can see, took me a long time to carve. All of this was taught to me by papa Abrahán, whom they have always favored for being very skillful; that is where the recommendation comes from, which Mama Martina got for me when she introduced me to her acquaintance Doña Micaela del Castillo, who is the wife of Don Melchor. They say he is a very demanding and hardworking gentleman; his assistant respects him and, above all, learns a great deal, since he devotes himself to painting and building. It seems he is currently drawing up the plans for the church of San Lorenzo. If you like, you can come with me these days to deliver these works to the Church of San Francisco, where they are painting some pictures. Antoñito, surprised and full of admiration, gave a shout: of course! I'm eager to meet that gentleman they call "Golden Brush." How did you hear about that? I heard some Spaniards say they had seen him painting, in the community of Puna, some canvases of the Virgin's flight into Egypt, and on that occasion they spoke of him by that name, or pseudonym. Ah, uncle Rafael, and these coffins? He answered: I was forgetting, they are orders from Don Agapito, and I'm leaving this for you to earn something: sand it and then varnish it, you're good at that, get to it right now. Without another word I set to work until late at night. I had to do the body and the lid with care. My arms were all numb, I could no longer move them, I felt tired, and I decided to finish the next day and then get on with the varnishing; for that I am preparing the stain, my brushes and the varnish.

The next day, at dawn, I applied the stain to the two coffins, and by midday the varnishing was finished. I was only waiting for uncle Rafael's approval, and afterwards those in charge of the funeral were to take them away.

One Holy Thursday at midday, my uncle Rafael and I were making our way to the Church of San Francisco, carrying the carved, gilded frames. We climbed the steps; my legs were trembling, I began to sweat, and I felt as if I had to face some great ordeal, but my curiosity to meet that gentleman was so great. We passed under the lintel of the second gate and heard a very hoarse voice say, God's good day to you. At that instant my whole body shuddered, and we answered together: good day, Don Nico, how are you? He replied: very well, excellent, I like your punctuality and your work; later I'll show it to the master, he is very busy with the commissions from the Franciscan fathers. After walking a few steps I saw a painting that left me frozen. Look, uncle, who is that saint? He has such a strong gaze, and he is holding the child; all he lacks is speech. At that moment Don Nico told us: don't talk loudly, it bothers the master. What you are looking at is a commission; it is Saint Matthew the Evangelist, shown writing in his book at the angel's command. I was so struck by the color of the skin, by his expression of a great thinker, as though he were even possessed by another spirit and receiving messages or orders, a mandate that he transcribes with his quills, by the colors of the mantle and all his surroundings, so that it seemed you were inside the picture. Antoñito, what's the matter, you've frozen... Forgive me, Don Nico, how real this painting is.

Don Nico, in a moment of rest while waiting for new orders, began to tell us: Master Melchor is very busy. He is from the valley and paints only on commission. He says he was taught by a Spaniard called Murillo and another called Zurbarán. It is the tata curas (the priests) who trained him and have supported him all along. He says he has lived with the priests since he was very small and received all his guidance and education from them; because of his talents and intelligence they sent him to Spain, where he stayed a long time, coming back already well trained and devoting himself to the fathers' commissions. He traveled everywhere at the demand and request of the churches and of some families of the Viceroy. But what I notice is that some days he falls silent and seems downcast. One afternoon I found him lying on the floor, trembling; he only asked me for hot tea, and you could hear him coughing hard, over and over. I hope it doesn't get worse. I beg him, telling him not to stay up all night, to rest. He doesn't listen to me, he works so much, he doesn't like to go out walking. If something happens to him, what would become of me? Because I have grown used to him and learned a lot from him. What I think is that when we travel by mule day and night it wears him out. Other times we rest along the way, and many times we spend the night in very barren, cold places; we sleep on llama hides to withstand the very low temperatures, and on top of that we don't eat well. Besides, when we prepare his paints we grind earths or ochres and breathe in a lot of dust, above all the one who does the finest part, which has to be to his liking. What is impressive is that when he has new commissions for paintings for the convents and monasteries, he stays shut in his room for days in order to settle his inspirations, which finally become his paintings, which are impressive, like Saint Jerome, Saint Francis of Paola, Saint Matthew and others. When you see them you are very impressed; they look like living people, and they frighten me a lot, especially when I walk at night. It seems as if they are watching me, and I even think they are accusing me of something, and I start to wonder what wrong I have done…

While I was waiting for my uncle and Don Nico to return, for they had gone to buy some materials, sitting pensively in the doorway, a gentleman of lordly bearing suddenly appeared before me, serious, with a deep gaze, looking almost angry, and he asked me: what are you doing sitting there, boy, who brought you? I had to explain my reasons and why I was in that place. Having heard me, I told him that we had brought the frames that he, sir, had ordered. He calmed down and, with a smile, answered me in a hoarse, confident voice: for many years I have not had the chance to talk with someone your age, and I like it, I even feel a spiritual peace. At that instant I took the opportunity to ask him: Master, Master, and where did you learn to paint these marvels, marvels… Don't be surprised, son; they are the expression of what is inside me, and I do it with such love and commitment because I live that reality with them. No wonder, Master, it seemed to me they really look at you, and all that's missing is for them to ask me something. Ha, ha, they are saints of the holy book, and commissions from the church. As I told you, I feel at peace, and I can tell you a little of my story. It began many years ago, when I was very small. It seems I was born in the church; for as long as I can remember I was always with the tata curas. I liked to draw, and that was the reason why, at your age, the fathers sent me to Spain on a ship, bound for a convent that was a school of art. There I stayed and met my master Bartolomé. For the first years I had no contact with him, only with his disciples, who were older men, such as Meneses and Osorio. They gave all of us who were beginners the task of grinding ochres of many colors and mixing them with oils, from the dark colors to the light ones, warm as well as cool. They were so demanding about the fineness of the grinding of the terracottas that the work necessarily went on to be graded or approved by other senior men, almost next in rank to the master, and sometimes it was rejected at the very moment it was being applied to the canvases. Once this stage of tasks was over and done, only then did we devote ourselves to drawing sketches on cloths, which we had to clean in order to use them again. After 6 years of this work, only then did I come close to the master, and it was possible thanks to the recommendation given to him by the Franciscan father who made the voyages to the Americas, accompanying the Spanish sailors who carried slaves on the King's orders.

My first use of the brush, with so much fear, was with Maestro Meneses. He guided me very well, and many times he asked me to paint certain segments, valuing my skill above all, though I was not to mention it to my companions. And so it went on, year after year, until I had great dexterity; I took advantage of the master's absences. He traveled a great deal, his presence was requested in other places, and we did not see him for long stretches. My master used to say that rich people from many countries made great demands of him. And so the years went by. I felt very happy to be fulfilling my dreams and doing what I longed to do. This is part of what I did and learned… well, up to now that I have told it to you, and I don't know why, and I don't even know your name or where you are from… Forgive me, maestro, my name is Antoñito, I am the grandson of Doña Martina and the nephew of Don Rafael, the master carpenter. Yes, I already know him through his works, which are fantastic. And your parents… Don Primo and Mama Catalina. How wonderful. Respect them and love them above all things; time passes, and so often we cannot value what we have and what they did for us. Don't forget, come and visit me. I am glad to have shared these moments; come whenever you like. Thank you very much, maestro, for me it is a joy to meet you, and above all an honor. No, the honor is mine… And deep inside I kept repeating, how wise this gentleman is, what an intense satisfaction. That soft voice echoed in my mind again and again, and I felt as if I were walking on clouds. I am glad to have shared these moments, come whenever you like… that is, I was as if I were dreaming, dreaming, and suddenly I sensed a silence and saw him leaning back in his armchair, in a deep sleep. He looked very worn out, and I stayed there contemplating his figure. After a while I heard the footsteps and voices of my uncle and Don Nico, who was surprised to see him beside me. Don't make any noise, let him rest, he is very tired, he works until very late. In any case, boy, thank you very much for looking after him. We left at once, and he reminded my uncle to be ready for any call. We walked a long way in silence, and he asked me, did you talk with the maestro? And with some effort I answered yes. What did he talk to you about? And I told him: about his art and where he was trained. For me it was a marvel and an honor that he spoke with me. How good, Antoñito, may it serve you as a lesson for life. Thank you, uncle, thank you for taking me to meet these honorable gentlemen, so honest and so humble…
Days later, he still could not forget, and Maestro Holguín's words kept resounding in his mind.
All in a hurry, he went to San Francisco and looked for Don Nico. Please, señor, I would like to ask you a favor… What's the matter, boy? I want to bring the gentleman a present… something my mama

Martina made… I'll ask, and you come tomorrow before he starts his work… Very well, Don Nico. At dawn he prepared his little bag with the buñuelos his sister Nelly had made for him and set off for the church. He turned the handle, and Don Nico, with some effort, opened the great door with a dull creak. Come in, son, come in. He is at the end of the corridor… Thank you, Don Nico… It was a workshop lit brightly by candles. Good morning, maestro, I have brought you this present, some buñuelos. Why, son, what is this? They look delicious, and they're warm, let me try one… how delicious, you'll have to bring me some often… Yes, maestro… Last time you told me you would like to be a painter. You are someone I trust deeply. You know, painting is not only imitating form, but giving a voice to the silence of our ancestors. Every brushstroke is also an act… of memory of life itself, and color reminds me that all true learning is born of sensitivity and respect for those who came before us. Therefore every painting expresses the secret and the wisdom of those who lived before. In the same way he spoke of the lives of the ancestors and of the value of connecting what is seen with what is not seen. He taught me that teachings are carried across time, and that the memory of the past lives in every gesture and every thought. I could understand very little of it at that moment.

Mama Martina's dreams and her real life met in that last memory: the inheritance of love, of memory and of wisdom. Antonito understood that every act of respect and affection toward our ancestors is also an act of creation and continuity. I am because they were, and I will be for as long as I remember them….
The Treasure of Don Francisco Rocha

It was the year 1642 in the Villa Imperial, which was at the height of its mining boom. At that time the silver mills (ingenios) covered the slopes of the mountain and both banks of the river, rising above massive granite walls. In the towers turned the master wheel and the iron balls that ground to powder the ore extracted from the mines. The owner of Thuru Cancha, one of the finest mills along the river, was Don Francisco Rocha. And he was not truly a Don… because that title had not been granted to him by the Sovereign Will of the Monarch, but because he had a great deal of money, which took the place of the parchments that purified Plebeian blood. He was content with his blood: if it was not the blue blood of the Nobility, it was the red blood of the descendants of Tupac Katari. He could have covered every street and square of Potosí with silver, and what set him apart was that he was very generous and humble with the poor and with the Indians. They say that Don Francisco Rocha was a miner and silver merchant, a counterfeiter of coins; they considered him an adventurer, because he defied the Church and the Crown in his wish to change history, trying to correct wrongdoing and to make his own justice. He tried to improve the lives of the Indigenous people, but in doing so he also made Basque enemies. It is said that he was responsible for diverting to his own storehouses half of the silver that was supposed to be carried to the mint in Argentina. The townspeople swear that he had dealings with little goblins; some say they heard voices and the tramp of horses. The rich despised him because they doubted the source of his wealth; besides, he was a young man of mestizo origin whose fortune was dazzling, and their hatred grew all the more because he lived with a very beautiful Indian woman named Koricosichi. His dearest collaborators were Satuko, an Indigenous leader, and Quemar, an African prince captured as a slave by Spanish bands. One fine day, while Don Francisco Rocha was doing his shopping in the town, he was dazzled by a lady newly arrived from Spain. Making use of his gifts as a Don Juan and his skills as a gallant, he managed to make her his sweetheart, and she, very worldly and ambitious, went along with his requests and his offers to give her everything she might desire: pearls, diamonds and gold. Then one night she accepted what he had promised, and he took her in a carriage, her eyes covered with a scarf, on a journey with no known direction. She could only hear the mules galloping over the cobblestones, a sound that later grew hoarser, and finally the noise of a great door opening. They went on for a while longer in the darkness, and she was consumed by curiosity about where he was taking her. At last the scarf was removed, and in her amazement all she could do was let out a cry: they had entered his cave, and with great surprise she saw an immense treasure, chests of gold and silver coins, scattered brilliants and dunes of silver. He offered to give her the very best if she would be his companion, and as a token of his esteem she received a gold jewel set with brilliants. But she, not satisfied and with a cunning spirit, was very pensive throughout the return journey, on which her face was again covered so that she could never remember the direction or the route to the place she had been. After leaving that place she was set down in a very narrow street, from which she made her way to her lodging. Without losing any time, and in keeping with agreements made with her patrons, she went to a group of Basques and told them everything that had happened, step by step, detail by detail, the whole course of the journey on which she had seen such riches. Her listeners were left open-mouthed, and, driven even more by their own greed, they denounced him to the authorities, who had long been trying to capture him. One day, when that woman had arranged to meet him, he was taken prisoner on the grave charge of COUNTERFEITING COINS. Rocha, astonished and angry, was taken to the premises of that court, where, ruled by hatred and envy, they decided swiftly and capriciously on the harshest and most exemplary punishment, and he was then sentenced to death by all those Basque enemies. In the name of the Crown he was executed: they hanged him and left him lying in the street, where many days later he was taken up by his wife. How great was her shock to see her beloved utterly disfigured, covered in wounds, his neck shattered, already showing signs of decay. Taking advantage of the night, and above all because no one passed that way, she lifted him and took him in her arms as if her beloved's weight were nothing, and carried him in a wooden cart, covering him with her shawl, amid sobs and weeping, swearing again and again that she would take revenge on those who had committed such a crime. The echo of her weeping and her cries rang through the darkness and against the great mountain walls, and, as if they understood, some foxes and other animals could be heard howling. When she reached their hideaway, he was laid on a carved stone inlaid with gold and silver that sometimes served as a table on which to set down saddlebags, blankets, saddles and the gear of their journeys. She embraced him and screamed in despair, her cries resounding through the cave, and she told her helpers to find the herbs and powders to care for the remains of her lord. Without even noticing how much time had passed, the widow was woken by the servant, who told her that everything was ready to be applied to Don Francisco's body. There was a very pleasant scent of mint and of other plants known only to her people. Alone, her eyelids badly swollen, she undressed the body, bathed it and applied the powders over every part of it, so that no one would learn the secret and the skill with which her beloved was preserved. Afterward he was dressed in his finest clothes, embroidered with threads of silver and gold, and surrounded with part of his treasures and diamonds, which sparkled in the light of the torches placed beside him. It was at that moment that her mind filled with how to begin her revenge. Weeping as she-wolves do when they have lost their mate, she took her hair, which fell to her waist, black and gleaming like jet, as the ñustas (Inca princesses) wear it, or ccoricusichi, as her beloved used to call her. Taking a sharp knife, she cut it from the nape of her neck, gathering it from both sides, and hour after hour, taking lock after lock and pouring all her rage into it, she wove a very long rope, as strong as the chumpis (woven belts) that hold the ore for carrying. This will be the rope with which she pays for my suffering, she who robbed me of my hope, for whom I lost my whole world and my dreams. I swear by my gods that for what she took from me, my light, my dream, my path, my companion, I will take my revenge, and I will do it very soon. One night, driven by rage and grief, she set out for the town by the chosen, secret path, in a carriage, dressed in her beloved's clothes. She left the carriage on the outskirts, and for days she asked questions and watched the house of the woman who had caused her beloved to be seized by the guards and his enemies. And one night, when she was already physically exhausted, she recognized her and followed her, creeping up as stealthily as a leopard, and with all her strength she covered the woman's face and threatened her with death if she called for help. The woman resisted, and she struck her a hard blow that knocked her unconscious; then she carried her on her shoulders like a load of ore to the carriage, where she covered her and tied her hands and feet. So the lady who had caused it all was kidnapped and taken to the cave, where the remains of her beloved lay in vigil. Between tears and rage, with great effort, she sealed the entrance of the cave in the mountain with rocks and lime mortar, repeating insistently to her prisoner: you will die here with me, you deceived him, you lied out of greed, you were the cause of the death of my beloved, my dear one, my Francisco. From that day on, no one has ever known where Rocha's treasure lies. Every Potosí resident, whenever a wall is knocked down or the ground is dug up, hopes to come upon Rocha's treasure, or a tapado (a hidden cache), or some concealed colonial treasure that might be recovered at any moment: the wealth that great Potosí possessed, which lies beneath the earth and which other greedy outsiders could never get their hands on. But Rocha hid it and kept it for himself, in his house, they say, in a cave or in a house with a second courtyard, beneath a dome that stands in the village of Mondragón, a place that comes alive thanks to this treasure. And they even tell that the priest and the sacristan found it and were lost in the Devil's Cave. Some residents say the Tapado lies roughly 18 kilometers from the city, near the lagoons of Tarapaya and the Devil's Cave. (Sketch of the area.) From that date and year onward, locals and outsiders alike have searched for this treasure.
The Devil's Bridge

Jaime and Ricardo, the older brothers, were very busy and could not be present at the prize-giving, which was considered the most important one, because they had set aside those days for some mining work and, above all, to accompany their friends Alfredo Buhezo, Willy Varela and Walter Morales, who were devoted to searching for the traces, the trail left by the people close to the richest miner of all, Francisco Rocha, who had always boasted of owning brilliants, jewels, diamonds and gold and silver coins, and who had many times promised the people of the Villa that he would adorn the streets with silver, just to obtain the rank of gentleman. This was one of their goals: to find, by any means, ROCHA'S TREASURE… They would disappear for several days and turn up with pale faces and grown thin, which was a great worry for their parents. Each time they were asked, they repeated that they had been out in the Mondragón area, where Varela's father had his fields of corn, broad beans and potatoes, which were brought into town to be sold and eaten. That was only an excuse. As soon as day broke, their thoughts were wholly devoted to, or taken up with, being in the area of the Devil's Bridge, believing from rumors that it would be the place where one of the objects of their search was to be found. Others were drawn by the tapados, the hidden caches or chests that Spaniards had buried when they left Potosí for a time and, often for all sorts of reasons, never came back, so that they were forgotten. These riches were the focus not only of their attention but of many fortune seekers, just as in the days of mining and silver. For them it was a way to improve their economic situation, which had always been a great worry for their parents. They saw with their own eyes how their parents earned a living with great sacrifice and risk: risk from the work they did, while their pay did not justify the effort they made. They worked in the mines all day long, and their fortnightly wages barely covered food and a few clothes. Sometimes they would repeat what they thought: education is good, but it does not answer our needs.

Speaking of the Devil's Bridge, a place where the local people prayed as they crossed, especially as night was falling, what no doubt came to mind was one of the events the old people of the area used to tell, from which the place takes its name, the result of a story that happened there.

In the group of explorers, so as not to take the wrong paths, as had often happened to them, they asked for the help of one of the farmhands, who knew every imaginable corner of the region. They called him Albertico, and just as they reached the Devil's Bridge he would begin to tell one of the legends of the region, a love story between two young people. On hearing these words, they say, the whole group drew close and paid attention as never before, far more than to their parents' advice. He would begin, as all legends do, by saying: there was once a very handsome young peasant who fell in love with a very beautiful girl, the daughter of the corregidor (magistrate), and they saw each other in secret. But one day they were discovered by her father, who threatened him and laid down the following demand: if you want my daughter, you must pay me her dowry, which is this amount of silver, within one year; otherwise you will never see her again. I do this because I have heard that you work hard and well, never forgetting what family you come from. This time starts today. In that very short time, the suitor pledged to keep this promise, and to do so he began to work at many things, as a miner, a helper, a carrier of ore. And up close he saw how the workers labored, facing many dangers: cave-ins, falls into mine shafts, and often being trapped in the workings. And most surprising of all, they ate almost nothing; they only chewed coca, which allowed them to work without tiring. And on one of those afternoons he saw the remains of a miner brought out after an accident, and heard the endless weeping of his small children and his wife, which truly awakened an intense sadness. A year later, having earned the dowry, on the day of his return with what he had earned, to fulfill the agreement with his sweetheart's father, he set out with his donkey and came to a ravine he had to cross. Suddenly the sky turned dark, as if to foretell a conflict; thunder crashed, and lightning lit up the whole place, and a torrential rain began, with the roar of waterfalls and the grinding of rocks being swept along, numbing the senses. And he asked himself: what am I going to do now, how will I reach the town, it is impossible to cross, what can I do? Her father will not believe my word, and it will be his reason to forbid me to see her. In his despair an uncontrollable rage rose in him; he kicked the rocks and pounded the edge of the gorge, weeping, shouting, amid lightning and a terrifying, overwhelming din. What can I do now? I feel powerless and I have no hope left. And finally, into his confused mind, with no other choice or option left, came the idea of asking the devil for help, and in a loud voice he spoke the following words: [ I would even give my soul if he would help me build a bridge. At that very instant, to his great surprise, the devil appeared with a thunderous crash and a certain smell of burnt sulfur, standing right before him, with a hoarse voice that grated on the ears and an air of arrogance and self-assurance, hearing his request. What do you want from me, why did you call me? You know that if I do it, it is on one condition: when I finish what you ask, I will take your soul. The young man told him: build a stone bridge. And without further ado he accepted, on that condition: if it is finished by dawn, before the rooster crows, my soul will be yours. I agree, but keep it in mind… before the rooster crows… It's a deal. In his extreme haste the devil cut the stones and set to work as if he were dozens of workers building the bridge. The young man, calmer and more at peace, began to reflect and realized the mistake he had made, and he asked God for help: Lord, forgive me for this act; I didn't know what to do in my haste, and my anxiety made me commit this madness. Please help this poor son of yours who is caught in this misfortune. And suddenly he perceived a sign, white like a radiance: the archangel Saint Gabriel. At that moment there was a clap of thunder and a flash of lightning, and he wondered, could this be the sign my Lord is giving me? Then he felt a shudder run through his body, and an inner peace, no longer the despair that had gripped him. Suddenly, on the horizon, there were signs that dawn would soon come. He saw the devil hurrying to take the last stones to finish the edges of the bridge, and suddenly many angels appeared who kept the devil from lifting the stones and setting the final stage in place to complete it. And far off could be heard the sharp sound of the rooster's first crow at dawn. The demon, defeated, spitting sparks and thunder, vanished into the infinite, saying: I will not forgive you.. In this way the young man saved his soul, and the bridge was left unfinished, but it no longer kept him from fulfilling his promise of the silver. And so his pledge was fulfilled, and with it the couple's dream came true: the marriage of the two young people, who lived happily for a long time, with several children.

chapters.title: The Farewell of Doña Martina, the Midwife

blocks.text: Weary now from her labors and from caring for her family, Doña Martina and her husband, Don Abrahán, decide to set out on a very long journey. But first they gather all the members of the family at their house, as was their custom, to share some lamb broth and chicha prepared by the expert hands of the lady of the house. Rafael, the eldest son, cheerful as always, turns up with some of his friends from work, armed with their string instruments and small drums, and they sing with one voice, in high and low tones, and this is how it went.
Un puñal envenenado atravesaste mi pecho
blocks.note: A sorrowful love song of heartbreak and longing that Rafael and his friends sing at the farewell gathering (kept in the original Spanish).

blocks.text: Ondas huellas has dejado en mi corazón desecho de amor
Ondas huellas has dejado en mi corazón desecho de amor
Al cielo pido la muerte y él no me la quiere dar
Me parece que hasta el cielo se goza y se goza de verme llorar
Dime si me quieres o si voluntad me tienes
Dime, dime si me quieres o si voluntad me tienes
Donde caben voluntades el amor ya puede caber.

I dedicate this song to my mamita Martina. Ever since I was little, I remember, I always saw her working, day and night. It didn't matter if it was cold or raining, she went out and came back in the early hours of the morning, all worn out, and always, always with her gifts: a lamb, some hens, or her fruit. The same with my papa Abrahán, with his carpentry and carving work, which I learned from him, and with what patience he taught me! Today I can earn my living and make my way with it. To them we dedicate these two songs, and as I try to begin, my throat tears apart and I feel like crying out loud, but today I will be brave. With all my heart I dedicate these two songs.
El pintaba paredes y otro lucia
blocks.note: A tender song about a gentle, loving father, which Rafael dedicates to his parents Martina and Abrahán (kept in the original Spanish).

blocks.text: El pintaba la cuna que yo dormía
Y cantaba bajito acariciando
Valsecitos milongas y algunos tangos
Y cantaba bajito acariciando
El mateaba debajo del limonero
Los domingos de junio de abril a enero
Y miraba la vida desde una sonrisa
Enseñaba a vivir la vida con valentía
Él hablaba el idioma de la ternura
Con pocas palabras y mil dulzuras
Pero siempre recuerdo a lo lejos

It surprises me that at just one word of invitation you have all come to my farewell. I see my comadres, my godchildren, my neighbors, and also Doña Casimira and her relatives. You have all filled me with your gifts and food. Thank you all. But what is happening? I see some of you crying, with such sad faces. Don't be like that, you'll make even me and Abrahán cry. This moment of farewell had to come sooner or later. We still have strength and, above all, the fighting spirit we won in this holy land, where my children were born, and my dreams, and I am above all proud to have earned the esteem and affection of each one of you.

You all know my Rafito. With his music and singing, he tried to express his feelings of love and, of course, of sadness; you can see it in his tears over our leaving. He and my daughters should feel happy, because they have been the reason for our lives. We have given them all our love and sacrifice. Above all, they have seen and felt how we faced very sad and hard situations, which all of us endured in our own flesh: they, deprived of our presence, responsible for the food and for supporting their brothers and sisters together; we, doing our part to settle everything that was pending day after day, many times receiving only water. We came back with joy and above all with hope, and all of that was reflected in our children, who welcomed us with laughter and tears. That is how we have shaped them, with dreams, joy, sadness, effort, failure, stumbling and getting up again with the same strength, and guided them along the path they should follow according to their own outlook and interests. They are strong and able to face any setback. I also want to take this moment to praise and admire my son-grandson Antoñito, who from a very young age showed every interest in being by our side, offering himself for any task, helping his grandfather Abrahán as best he could, learning the skills of carpentry and carving. And with me, what can I say, he would not leave my side. He followed me to watch how I treated the sick and to walk long distances for long stretches of time. Afterwards you could see how tired he was, and in his little voice he would tell me, Mamita, I can't go on, my little feet hurt. We took the chance to rest and eat our mote de haba and piri. After our rest we managed to pick out and gather many plants, roots and medicinal earths. We came back from that walk much calmer, as I explained to him what they were for and how they were prepared. He asked questions all the time, he was never quiet, and we were satisfied at having found and obtained what we needed for our purposes. What a joy to see my comadres, neighbors and close friends who were my patients come to this, my request and my farewell. All of you, sooner or later, will have to follow the same path, a path we have walked day after day, with or without guidance, with hardships or great satisfactions. I don't want to remember my childhood. The only thing I can tell you is that I worked and learned a great deal, from people, from Doña Aurora de la Cruz, from the old world of Toledo, whom I consider my mother. My parents, whom I lost tragically, loved me very much. I am the product, the result, of my character and my perseverance. I also took on the habits and customs of the local people, which, of course, I passed on to my family.

All those present fell silent, and some were weeping, their faces full of sadness. From the crowd one of them rose and, in a broken voice, said, Doña Martina, we consider you a mother. Every time we came to you, by day or by night, you never turned down our request, whether for health, for advice, or even for food. Today, as you leave us, you leave us with a very deep sorrow. We greatly admire the family you leave behind, and we do not doubt that they will fill your absence. Not all of us are here today; wherever we go, people ask about you, Mama Martina. Our eternal gratitude, may the Lord be with you, and from afar pray for us. Each of us carries you in our heart and soul. May you live forever…. So ended this gathering, and everyone said goodbye slowly, down to the very last, in the gloom of the night.
At dawn, after giving a kiss to each of their children, who were sound asleep, they set out on a road to no fixed destination, never to return……

chapters.title: Note of Clarification, Acknowledgment and Dedication

blocks.text: This history, tale and legend, which goes back to the years 1600 to 1800 in the Imperial Town (Villa Imperial) of Potosí and the mines of Atocha and Tela Mayo, Tupiza and Tasna, is nothing more than the transcription of what my grandparents, Doña Martina and Abrahán, lived through… It is a partial compilation from Spanish literature, from the Potosí chronicler Bartolomé Arzans in his book History of the Imperial Town of 1705, from the chronicles of Potosí, and from the tale and legend of the dreams and fantasies of the protagonists who recounted all the events of the past and the paths they followed in these rich lands so full of history. May it remain in our memory as a memorable past of effort and sacrifice, remembering our forebears with affection and respect, so that it is not forgotten and endures through time. National songs and songs from northern Argentina are also included, which tell and interpret the reality of those times with simplicity and deep feeling. My thanks for this to everyone who has contributed to this work, dedicated to my grandparents, my parents and my dear and unforgettable family… May 1, 2020. Buenos Aires–Cochabamba.

Freddy Córdova Ossio was born in Potosí, Bolivia, in 1943. He studied at the Colegio Pichincha and graduated from the School of Fine Arts of Tomás Frías University in Potosí. He trained as a general physician at the Universidad Mayor de San Simón in Cochabamba, and specialized in Pediatrics and Public Health at the Pereira Rossell Hospital of the Universidad Oriental del Uruguay. He later specialized in Pediatric Surgery at the Ricardo Gutiérrez Children's Hospital in Buenos Aires, Argentina. During his professional life he was a rural and emergency physician at the Eduardo Eguía Hospital in Tupiza, and a consulting physician for Codex and for the Andean Rural Health Council. He is a former director of the Bolivian-Japanese Technical School of Health and of Pediatrics at the Solomon Klein Hospital, and was Professor of Pediatrics and head of the Department of Social and Family Medicine at the UMSS Faculty of Medicine. His most recent works include: Health Proposals; New Models of Care; Public Health and the UMSS; The Faculty of Medicine and the Community; The Crisis of Adolescence; and Primary Care as a Model of Care at the Nueva Gante Health Center (UMSS). Health researcher at the South Group Research Institute, Cochabamba.
